Normal.

CHAPTER 123
THE COMPANION

Lyssa found me buying pears.

This was inconvenient because I had already rejected two pears for being soft and was examining a third with more seriousness than fruit deserved.

“You look suspicious.”

I looked up.

Lyssa stood on the other side of the stall with a wrapped bundle tucked under one arm.

She was taller than the woman beside her, thinner than most of the crowd, her hair catching the morning light around her head.

“I am purchasing fruit.”

“Exactly.”

The pear seller looked between us.

“I don't want to know.”

“You do,” Lyssa said.

“I don't.”

I bought the pear.

Lyssa waited until we had moved away from the stall.

Then she held out her hand.

“For what?”

“The pear.”

“I bought it.”

“I found you.”

“That does not establish ownership.”

“It establishes a fee.”

“You are becoming like the keeper.”

“Terrifying.”

I gave her the pear.

She took one bite.

“This is good.”

“I know.”

“You tested it?”

“I inspected it.”

“You touched three.”

“Two failed.”

She laughed. Pear thief.

I had not seen her in several days.

That was long enough for the fact of her to feel new for about half a second.

Then not new.

Better.

“What are you doing?” I asked.

“Working.”

She lifted the bundle.

“What is it?”

“Cloth.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why ask?”

“Destination.”

“North side.”

“Paid?”

“Yes.”

“Time?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That one was almost normal.”

“I am improving.”

“No.”

Fair.

She took another bite of my pear.

“Where are you going?”

“This is breakfast?”

“No. This is pear.”

“Good distinction.”

“I had not selected the rest.”

“Come with me.”

“North side?”

“Yes.”

“That is the opposite direction from the food I wanted.”

“Then don't.”

She kept walking.

I followed.

This was not difficult.

Not physically.

The north-side streets were busier than I preferred at that hour, but the grade was mild and the paving mostly intact.

Lyssa did not slow herself into a performance.

She also did not disappear.

She walked.

I walked.

Sometimes she was half a pace ahead.

Sometimes beside me.

At one corner a cart blocked most of the crossing, and she went through the narrow gap before realizing my crutches would not fit comfortably.

She stopped on the other side.

I went around the back of the cart.

When I reached her, she said:

“Sorry.”

“Why?”

“I picked the stupid gap.”

“Yes.”

“You could say it's fine.”

“It was fine.”

“You could say that before agreeing it was stupid.”

“Both can be true.”

She shook her head.

We continued.

At the next crossing a delivery wagon had stopped crooked, leaving a strip of paving between its rear wheel and a stack of baskets.

Lyssa looked at the gap.

Then at me.

“I'm learning.”

“Congratulations.”

She went around the front instead.

That route was longer but wide.

I followed.

“Was that correct?” she asked.

“There is no test.”

“Pessa would hate that answer.”

“Pessa would hate the question.”

“Who is Pessa?”

I looked at her.

“You have not met Pessa?”

“I've heard the name.”

“Movement.”

“That explains nothing.”

“Your movement?”

“Sometimes.”

“Does she like you?”

“No.”

“Then probably.”

“That is not how liking works.”

“It is with some people.”

I thought of Pessa refusing to tell me what she measured.

Maybe.

No.

Separate.

“That sounds threatening.”

“It is mostly dirt.”

“Terrifying.”

We continued.

No lesson.

Good.

“Still there.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“I have been going.”

“I know.”

“Jorren?”

“Jorren.”

Traitor.

“What did he say?”

“That you read something.”

“That is broad.”

“That people yell at you.”

“That is also broad.”

“That you keep going back.”

“Yes.”

She glanced at me.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

I waited for the rest.

There wasn't any.

This was one of Lyssa's better habits.

She could ask a question and then not turn the answer into a project.

Lyssa went inside.

I remained outside.

“You can come.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

“That is not the same answer.”

I considered.

She was probably better at this than me.

A woman behind a counter took Lyssa's bundle, untied it, checked the cloth, checked a small slip, and counted coins.

Not my business.

Not bad.

Just a second too long.

One for her.

Mostly.

Not broken.

Just dry.

Crutches against the stone.

No negotiation.

No chair.

No stairs.

Good.

No.

Not Pessa.

Child with hoop.

Airflow.

Copper.

REACH.

Natural enough.

Just hand.

Ordinary.

Good.

No.

Not precisely.

Enough.

She asked it casually.

I had several answers.

Theatre.

Guild.

Food.

Sit here.

Her.

That last one was not an activity.

Probably.

“Stay here.”

Lyssa nodded.

So we did.

This was extremely inefficient.

Lyssa took the second fried cake apart with her fingers instead of biting it.

“You're destroying it.”

“Yes.”

She waited.

This was a trap with an obvious answer.

I refused it on principle.

One had abandoned the hoop and was now trying to walk along the fountain rim with both arms out.

His friend followed.

A woman across the square told them to get down.

They ignored her.

She stood.

They got down.

Efficient authority.

No.

Not my problem.

Lyssa said, “Do you like me without proving it?”

There.

I looked at her.

She was smiling, but not entirely joking.

“Yes.”

The answer came before analysis.

That was rude.

To me.

Lyssa's smile changed.

Smaller.

“Good.”

“Yes.”

Easy.

She stared at me.

Probably.

Acceptable.

Warmth.

Ordinary phantom.

No magic.

Nothing needed doing.

“Yes.”

Not helping.

Not leaving.

I was going west.

Probably.

I pointed at her.

“No.”

She stepped closer.

Kissed me.

Not cheek.

Mouth.

Brief.

Easy.

“No.”

“Where?”

“Terrifying, isn't it?”

Not the kiss.

No.

Dangerous.

No.

Fruit.

My shoulders were fine.

Palms fine.

Right calf fine.

Residual limb quiet.

No magic.

“No.”

“No.”

toward forearm.

sideways.

BASELINE:
variable.

No.

CHAPTER 124
THE REPAIRMAN

The yellow bird was still on the table in the morning. This seemed correct. I left it there. My hands were normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the ordinary useless way, heel resting on a floor that did not exist.

No magic today. That was less offensive than yesterday. Not good. Less offensive. I ate. The keeper looked at my shirt. Gray. She frowned.

“What?”

“I've lost the system.”

“There was no system.”

“Green was theatre.”

“Once.”

“Blue was theatre too.”

“Yes.”

“Now gray.”

“I own several shirts.”

“This is becoming difficult.”

“For you.”

She pointed at me with a spoon.

“Where are you going?”

I considered lying for no reason.

“Theatre.”

She looked triumphant.

“That proves nothing.”

“It proves gray is theatre.”

“No.”

I left before she could classify trousers. The walk west was ordinary. That mattered because tomorrow morning would not be. Hessa. Thread. No. Theatre. I could think about a thread tomorrow. Probably for several hours while Hessa prevented me from touching one.

The theatre doors were open. Inside, something was roaring. I stopped. Not a beast. A man. Then another roar. Worse.

Someone shouted:

“Again.”

The roar came a third time. I went in. The servant actor was standing center stage with both hands around his mouth. He saw me.

“Gregory!”

The roar stopped.

“That was you?”

“Yes.”

“It was bad.”

“Fuck you.”

Teren, in his chair, looked over a page.

“Blue Shirt is back.”

“Gray.”

“Worse.”

The unnamed woman near the stage edge looked at me once.

“Ramp.”

“Yes.”

Nobody asked why I was there. Good. The broad grooved scenery ramp was partly blocked by a painted panel showing a stone garden wall. The soot-shirt worker was holding one end while another worker adjusted the bottom brace.

She saw me.

“Wait.”

I waited. They shifted it.

“Go.”

I went. This was apparently my role in stage traffic now. Wait. Go. Crutch. Foot. Chair. Useful vocabulary. I reached the audience-side floor. My previous chair was occupied by a basket of fake fruit.

The bad rocking chair was empty. I looked at it.

Teren said:

“Paper is gone.”

“I remember.”

He tossed me a folded scrap. I caught it badly against my chest.

“Left front.”

“Yes.”

I folded it twice and put it under the chair leg. Stable. Mostly. The roaring resumed. I watched. The servant actor tried again. This time he lowered the pitch. It sounded like a sick cow.

The woman said:

“No.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then why did you do it?”

“Commitment.”

“That is not a defense.”

Someone behind the scenery laughed. I looked at Teren.

“What are they doing?”

“Horse.”

I looked back at the servant actor.

“No.”

“Exactly.”

Onstage, a second actor crossed from the painted doorway carrying a letter. The woman pointed.

“From ‘I heard him at the south road.’”

The actor began.

“I heard him at the south road. He was riding like the dead had sent him back.”

The servant actor crouched just offstage and made the sick-cow sound. The actor onstage did not react. The woman stopped him.

“You heard a horse.”

“I heard him.”

“Then hear him.”

The actor reset. Again.

“I heard him at the south road. He was riding like the dead had sent him back.”

The roar. This time the actor looked toward the wing before continuing. Better. Still not a horse.

I said:

“Why is the horse roaring?”

Everyone looked at me.

The servant actor said:

“Because nobody can find the hoof board.”

“The what?”

Teren pointed with his page toward a pile backstage.

“Board with the cups.”

I stared. That explained nothing. The soot-shirt worker disappeared behind the garden wall.

The woman said:

“Again without it.”

The actor reset. The servant actor inhaled.

“No,” the woman said.

He lowered his hands.

“You have taken my only art.”

“You have several arts. Most are unfortunate.”

They ran the line without sound. The actor looked toward the wing. Nothing happened. It was worse. The woman frowned.

“Need something.”

“I said that,” the servant actor said.

“You are not something.”

“I am deeply wounded.”

The soot-shirt worker returned dragging a narrow board with four shallow wooden cups mounted beneath it. Two were cracked. One hung sideways.

“Found it.”

She put the board on the floor. The servant actor brightened.

“Horse.”

“That is not a horse,” I said.

He looked at me.

“You keep saying that.”

The worker picked up one end of the board and rocked it against the floor. Clop. Clop-clop. Clop. Oh.

“That is stupid.”

“Yes,” she said.

She rocked it faster. The uneven cups struck in sequence. The sound was not accurate. It was also immediately a horse. Annoying. They reset. The actor onstage began.

“I heard him at the south road. He was riding like the dead had sent him back.”

Clop. Clop-clop. Clop. The actor turned toward the wing. The servant actor stepped backward as though making space for something entering fast. The woman raised two fingers.

From behind the garden wall, another worker snapped a gray cloth low across a gap and released it. A dark shape crossed the opening for less than a second. Not a horse. Not even close.

The actor flinched aside. Teren turned a page. I saw a horse. Fuck. The scene continued.

“He nearly rode me down.”

The servant actor shouted from the wing:

“He still might.”

Audience laughter would go there. Probably. The woman let the scene continue another few lines. Then stopped.

“Again.”

I looked at the board. Then the cloth. Then the gap. The cloth had no legs. No head. It was approximately horse-colored. Maybe.

“That's it?”

The soot-shirt worker looked at me.

“What else do you want?”

“A horse.”

“No.”

“A better silhouette.”

“No.”

“The cloth is wrong.”

“No.”

“It doesn't have the correct shape.”

She picked up the board.

“Does it sound enough like a horse?”

“Not exactly.”

“Good.”

“That is not what good means.”

She walked away.

Teren said:

“You're still checking the cloth.”

“It's wrong.”

“And the scene still works.”

I watched them run it again. Clop. Gray movement. Actor reaction. Horse. Not real. Not even a convincing illusion. There was barely any illusion at all. The audience would know there was no horse.

Of course they would. They were in a theatre. That somehow made the problem worse. The actor missed his next line. Teren gave him the first three words. He caught it. The horse disappeared from my attention.

The scene lived. I hated this place. I stayed. After two runs, one of the wooden cups split completely.

The sound became:

Clop. Crack. Clop. The servant actor stopped.

“Dead horse.”

The woman said:

“Keep going.”

He looked at the broken board. The actor onstage had already started the line.

“I heard him at the south road.”

The soot-shirt worker kicked a small box. The servant actor grabbed it. He struck the side twice with his palm. Thump-thump. Wrong. The worker snapped the cloth. The actor looked. The servant actor clicked his tongue against his teeth.

Then slapped the box again in a faster rhythm. Not horse. Horse. The scene continued. Nobody stopped. I had been waiting for them to stop. They did not.

At the end the woman said:

“Better.”

The servant actor held up the broken cup.

“This died.”

“I saw.”

“Need another.”

“Later.”

She pointed at the actor.

“You looked too soon.”

“I heard the box.”

“You knew the box was coming. He didn't.”

She pointed toward the imaginary person inside the play. The actor frowned. Again. No lecture. No table. Again. The soot-shirt worker carried the broken board toward a worktable. I followed. Not immediately. That would have looked eager.

I waited maybe six seconds. Still eager. Fine. The board was simple. Four cups. Different depths. Mounted on short pegs beneath a narrow plank so rocking transferred weight unevenly. One peg had split.

“I can fix that,” I said.

The worker looked at me.

“No magic.”

I blinked.

“How do you know?”

“You talk.”

“That does not answer the question.”

“Hessa talks too.”

This was alarming.

“What did she say?”

“Nothing to me. Somebody said you're on no-magic.”

Carrow had achieved information transmission without my consent.

“I meant the peg.”

“You can fix wood?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She handed me the broken piece. I sat at the worktable. There were tools. Normal tools. Knife. Small hand drill. Cord. Glue. Wood scraps. The peg did not need magic. Good. I chose a scrap.

The original peg had been too thin. That was obvious. I cut a replacement thicker. The worker watched for approximately three seconds, decided I was not going to remove a finger, and left. Nobody supervised.

Also good. I shaped the peg. Too thick. Adjusted. Better. The hole in the cup was damaged. I could widen it. If I widened it, the cup would sit differently. That would alter sound.

I compared the other three. Different depths. Different angles. Not random. Probably. I measured by eye. Then with the edge of the knife. Then found a bit of cord and used that. Teren appeared beside the table.

“What are you doing?”

“Repair.”

“You look angry.”

“The cups are different.”

“Yes.”

“Intentionally?”

“No idea.”

He left. Useless. I tested the cup. The crack changed the sound. It should be replaced too. There were spare cups somewhere. Probably. I searched the shelf under the table. Three cups. One too deep.

One too shallow. One nearly right but heavier. I tapped each. The heavier one had better tone. Not the same tone. Better. This was now a design problem. I forgot the horse scene for several minutes.

The servant actor appeared.

“Horse doctor.”

“No.”

“Can it live?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“Not yet.”

He picked up the heavier spare cup.

“This one.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Different weight.”

He rocked it against the table. Clop.

“That sounds horse.”

“It changes the sequence.”

He rocked it again. Clop.

“Horse.”

“You are not helping.”

“I am the customer.”

“No.”

He left with the cup. I followed.

“You cannot just take it.”

He could. He had. The soot-shirt worker had already mounted the spare cup with cord. Not even the new peg. Cord. Ugly. Loose. Temporary. The board rocked. Clop. Clop-clop. Clop. The sequence was slightly different.

I could hear it. Nobody cared. The woman pointed.

“From south road.”

They ran it. The horse worked. Better than before. Not because the sound was more accurate. Because the actor waited this time. The gray cloth passed. The servant actor stepped aside late enough that it looked like something had actually forced him to.

The actor's eyes tracked the gap. The horse existed for about two seconds. Then it did not. The scene continued. I stood with my replacement peg in one hand. Unused. The soot-shirt worker looked at it.

“Good peg.”

“Yes.”

“Put it in the repair box.”

“It is for that board.”

“Later.”

“The cord will shift.”

“Probably.”

“The cup angle is wrong.”

“Probably.”

“It changes the sound.”

“Gregory.”

“Yes.”

“We have horse.”

I looked at the stage. They did. Fuck. I put the peg in the repair box. The worker went back to the wall flat. No philosophy. No explanation. Theatre had simply stolen my problem before I solved it.

I sat again. Teren tossed me a page.

“Hold.”

I held it. He had two versions open and was comparing a cut.

“What am I holding?”

“Page nine.”

“Why?”

“Because I have page eight and page ten.”

“That is not a reason.”

“It literally is.”

Fine. I held page nine. The woman cut two lines from the servant actor. He objected.

“They are my best lines.”

“They are your longest lines.”

“Same.”

“No.”

He appealed to Teren.

Teren said:

“I like the second one.”

“Traitor.”

The line stayed cut. Then came back. Then moved. I lost track. At some point Teren took page nine back without thanking me. Also normal. The horse board failed again after six runs. The cord slipped.

The cup rotated. I noticed first. I almost stood. Could not quickly anyway. The servant actor noticed second because the sound went wrong. He changed his hand position and made the next beat with the side of the board instead.

The actor reacted. Gray cloth. Horse. Scene continued. Nobody looked at the repair box. I did. The peg was still there. This felt personal. At break I retrieved it. The soot-shirt worker was eating something wrapped in paper.

I held up the peg.

“Now?”

She chewed.

“Sure.”

Victory. I installed it. The cup sat correctly. Mostly. I adjusted the angle. Rocked the board. The sequence was cleaner.

Closer to an actual four-beat pattern, though not exact because the mounted cups could not produce independent timing without more complex rocking. I could fix that. No. I stopped. The worker watched me stop.

“Done?”

“Yes.”

She rocked it. Clop. Clop-clop. Clop. She nodded.

“Good.”

That was satisfying. Then she took a small knife and shaved one side of my new peg. I stared.

“What are you doing?”

“Too tight.”

“It is secure.”

“It sticks.”

“That is secure.”

“We need to swap cups fast.”

“Why?”

“Different floor.”

I looked at her.

“What?”

“Stone stage sounds different than wood. Sometimes we use the shallow cup.”

Oh. She shaved it again. The peg still held. Looser. Removable. She handed me the knife.

“You want pretty or useful?”

“Those are not opposites.”

“Here they are.”

Then she walked away before I could argue. I hated her too. I did not know her name. This was becoming inconvenient. The afternoon continued. No grand event. No missing actor. No fire. No magical discovery.

There was an illusion of a window that turned blue when evening arrived in the play. I noticed it only because it flickered once. A worker behind the flat swore. The blue vanished. The scene kept going.

Someone adjusted a lamp. The painted window looked dimmer. Apparently that was enough until break. I wanted to know what failed. I did not ask. Not because I had developed restraint. I was still holding page nine.

Later, the blue returned. No announcement. No demonstration. Nobody cared except the person running it. Interesting. No. Not yet. The servant actor found me before I left.

“Horse doctor.”

“Stop calling me that.”

“Horse Gregory.”

“Worse.”

He handed me the board.

“What?”

“You made it work.”

“It already worked.”

He looked confused.

“Yes.”

That was somehow more insulting.

“Take it.”

“Where?”

“Back table.”

“You can carry it.”

“I am beloved.”

“That does not affect your arms.”

“It affects my obligations.”

I balanced the board awkwardly across my lap while seated. Then realized I could not carry it while using both crutches. He was already gone.

“Fuck.”

Teren passed. I pointed at the board. He took it without comment and put it on the back table. Then came back.

“Tomorrow?”

“Hessa.”

“Morning.”

“Yes.”

“After?”

“I don't know.”

“Good.”

“You all do that.”

“Do what?”

“Nothing.”

Teren looked at me for a moment. Then shrugged.

“Good.”

I left. My palms were warmer than yesterday by the time I reached home. Right calf mildly tired. Residual limb quiet. The phantom heel returned briefly on the stairs while the keeper spotted me.

Ordinary. No magic. The yellow bird was still on the table. I put the new image beside it in my head. Not literally. Horse board. Gray cloth. Actor looking toward nothing. Horse. The board had been broken.

They had used a box. The illusion window had failed. They had changed the lamp. Nothing had stopped. Tomorrow Hessa would ask me to make something happen correctly. Probably. Maybe. I looked at the yellow bird.

Then at my notebook. I did not write about the horse. I went to bed. For several minutes, I could still hear the wrong hoofbeats. They sounded enough like a horse.
CHAPTER 125
THE TEST CASE

Hessa had two threads. I disliked this immediately. They hung from the same wooden frame. Dark. Thin. One over the glazed tile beside the place my right forearm would go. The other farther away.

Not much farther. Enough. The gray cloth was folded on the side table. The copper was already out. Hessa was writing. I sat. She kept writing. I looked at the threads.

“Hands first,” Hessa said.

“I was observing.”

“Observe after I have your baseline.”

She finished the line.

“How are your hands?”

“Normal.”

“Right calf?”

“Normal.”

“Residual limb?”

“Baseline.”

“Phantom?”

“Ordinary.”

“Thumb?”

“Nothing.”

“Fingers?”

“Nothing.”

“Any urge to curl them?”

“No.”

“Wrist?”

“Normal.”

She held out her hand. I gave her mine. Right. She checked grip, thumb, fingers, wrist. Then left. Then residual limb.

Then the ordinary questions again in slightly different words because Hessa enjoyed catching lies I was not telling.

“Yesterday?”

“Theatre.”

“No magic?”

“No.”

“Day before?”

“Lyssa.”

“No magic?”

“No.”

“You understand that theatre using magic is not you using magic.”

“Yes.”

“Good. I asked because your face did something.”

“There was a window.”

“Greg.”

“I did not touch it.”

“Excellent.”

She went back to the table. I stared at the two threads.

“Why two?”

“Because one annoyed me.”

“That is not a scientific reason.”

“It is an excellent medical reason.”

“Hessa.”

She looked at me.

“The first test told me less about external effect than I wanted.”

“Yes.”

“It told me more about your control than I expected.”

“Yes.”

“That does not make the external result better.”

“I know.”

“You are saying that too quickly.”

“I still know.”

She pointed at the farther thread.

“This one is not for you.”

“Then why is it there?”

“For me.”

“That is irritating.”

“Good.”

She rolled my right sleeve above the elbow. The charcoal mark today was not the same. Still wrist-side. Slightly higher. A short line. Not the circle. Not the old line. New enough. I noticed.

Hessa tapped the new mark.

“Use today's line.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

She drew a second charcoal line on the glazed tile. One beneath each resting thread. The near thread hung approximately where the first had. The far one hung perhaps four inches beyond it. Both moved slightly while she worked.

One turned. Stopped. The other shifted sideways. Stopped. Hessa waited. I waited. She opened the door. Both moved. She closed it. Waited. She crossed the room heavily. The far thread trembled. Near one moved less.

She wrote.

“Table vibration,” I said.

“Maybe.”

“You walked near the far leg.”

“Yes.”

“On purpose?”

“Yes.”

She opened the window a finger width. Both threads shifted. Near first. Far second. She closed it.

“Air.”

“Yes.”

She stood beside the apparatus without touching it. The near thread drifted slightly toward her sleeve. Then away.

“Heat.”

“Maybe.”

“Static.”

“Maybe.”

“Why are we doing this again?”

“Because I am not asking the same question.”

I looked at the two threads.

“You are comparing them.”

“Yes.”

“That is the same question with a control.”

“No.”

“It is literally a control.”

Her mouth moved. Almost smile. Dangerous.

“What is the question?” I asked.

“Whether the thread closest to the altered region behaves differently from a second thread exposed to as much of the same room as I can manage.”

“That is a control.”

“Yes.”

“I said that.”

“You said it was the same question.”

“It is related.”

“Everything is related if you talk long enough.”

I considered the horse. Did not say it. Good. Hessa put the copper in position.

“Rules.”

“Minimal draw.”

“Yes.”

“Right forearm only.”

“Yes.”

“Small localized alteration at the marked region.”

“Yes.”

“Maintain underlying draw.”

“Yes.”

“If instructed, REACH from existing altered region only, smallest extension toward the near thread.”

“Yes.”

“No release.”

“Yes.”

“No push.”

“Yes.”

“No casting.”

“Yes.”

“No Barrier.”

“Yes.”

“No hand, wrist, finger movement.”

“Yes.”

“No increase in internal alteration.”

“Yes.”

“Stop if it feels like force.”

“Yes.”

“Stop if it broadens.”

“Yes.”

“Stop when you say stop.”

“Yes.”

“Far thread is not a target.”

“Yes.”

“No attempt to influence both.”

“Yes.”

“No attempt to compensate for room movement.”

“Yes.”

I paused.

“That last one was not in the first test.”

“No.”

“Because now there are two.”

“Because now you know enough to be dangerous in a boring way.”

“That is rude.”

“That is medicine.”

She had me breathe normally for several minutes. I watched. Near thread moved. Far thread moved. Sometimes together. Sometimes not. Once both shifted left almost simultaneously. Once the near thread moved toward my empty chair before I sat.

Useful. Annoying. Hessa wrote everything.

Then:

“Sit.”

I sat. Right forearm beside the near thread. Three quarters of an inch. Approximately. I did not measure. Hessa would kill me.

“Do not stare at the thread.”

“Where should I look?”

“My hand.”

She held two fingers above the copper.

“That is worse.”

“For you.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

I breathed. Ordinary. Phantom left heel present. No relevance. Right hand loose. No thumb. No fingers.

“Draw.”

I did. Minimal. Still strange. Less strange than months ago. More dangerous than it felt. Copper answered. Not strongly. Enough that Hessa watched it. Underlying draw stable.

“Shape.”

Small. Right forearm. Charcoal line. The altered response appeared. Localized. Slightly broader than the mark on the upper side. I reported it.

“Hold.”

I held. No motor. No thumb. No left change. Hessa watched.

“How certain?”

“High.”

“Not maximum?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She waited. Long enough that I started wondering whether this was the entire test.

Then:

“REACH.”

Smallest extension. Toward the near thread. Not force. Not push. Not more. Different. The near edge became more distinct. As before. The alteration felt asymmetric. Toward the thread.

“Near edge sharper,” I said.

“Continue same amount.”

Same amount was impossible. I attempted not to change what I was doing. Copper shifted. Hessa's eyes moved. Not to me. Past me. Probably thread. I did not look.

“Hold.”

I held.

“RETURN.”

Immediately. I reduced the altered response. Near edge softened. Center dimmed. No elbow shift. No urge. No wrist. Underlying draw remained.

“Hold.”

I held.

“Release.”

I released. Ordinary arm. Hessa touched my wrist.

“Open.”

I opened.

“Close.”

Closed.

“Thumb.”

Moved.

“Again.”

Fine. Then she let me look. Near thread rested slightly right of its charcoal line. Far thread rested slightly left of its line.

“What happened?”

“You tell me.”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

“You were not watching.”

“That was intentional.”

“Yes.”

“So tell me.”

She checked my forearm again before answering.

“During baseline, both moved repeatedly.”

“Yes.”

“During your draw, both moved once.”

“Together?”

“Near first. Far followed.”

“Air.”

“Maybe.”

“During shape?”

“Neither enough to record.”

“REACH?”

“The near thread moved toward your arm.”

My chest did something. Small. I hated that she saw it.

“The far thread?”

“Did not move at that moment.”

I stared. Hessa raised one finger.

“Keep it bounded.”

“What happened next?”

“While you maintained the same instruction, the near thread stopped. Then the far thread moved left.”

“Near?”

“Stayed.”

“So differential.”

“One differential observation.”

“Yes.”

“Then keep it at one.”

I looked at the near thread. It did not move. Of course.

“What does that mean?”

“Today?”

“Yes.”

“It means the nearer thread showed one movement toward your arm during REACH that the farther thread did not show at the same moment.”

“That is better.”

“Than what?”

“Than both moving.”

“Only if the question is whether they moved together.”

“The question is whether the near one behaved differently.”

“Yes.”

“It did.”

“Once.”

“Yes.”

“Then that is data.”

“Yes.”

“Useful data.”

“Yes.”

“Hessa.”

“It is more useful than the first test.”

There. I waited. She did not continue.

“And?”

“And I still cannot attribute it to mana.”

I exhaled. The far thread moved. Hessa pointed at it.

“That.”

I looked. It settled.

“Fuck.”

“Yes.”

“Could be breath.”

“Yes.”

“I was farther from that one.”

“Yes.”

“Could be convection.”

“Yes.”

“Static.”

“Yes.”

“Table vibration.”

“Yes.”

“Thread twist.”

“Yes.”

“Could be mana.”

“Yes.”

I looked at her. She looked back. That yes was worse than no.

“Then what changed?”

“My confidence that the test can produce interpretable information.”

Not my confidence that you moved it. Different. I knew. Still annoying. She tapped the farther thread lightly with a wooden stick. It spun.

“Last time, one thread moved and we had no local comparison.”

“Yes.”

“Today I saw a moment when the near thread behaved differently from the far thread.”

“Yes.”

“I also saw other moments when they behaved differently without magic.”

“Yes.”

“That matters.”

“Yes.”

I pointed at the apparatus.

“Why not put another thread the same distance on the other side?”

“Other side of what?”

“My arm.”

“Then it would not be exposed to the same local conditions.”

“It would be closer.”

“To different skin, different room position, different heat pattern, different movement.”

“Then put one on each side of the same altered region.”

“With what space?”

I looked. Not much.

“Smaller frame.”

“And now you have changed the frame.”

“That is solvable.”

“Yes.”

“So?”

“So I may do that later.”

I hated later. Hessa continued.

“Controls are not magic truth machines. They remove some explanations and leave others.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then say what today's second thread cannot tell us.”

I looked at it.

“It cannot tell us whether the near movement was mana.”

“Good.”

“It cannot fully match local heat.”

“Yes.”

“Or static.”

“Yes.”

“Or tiny air differences.”

“Yes.”

“Or thread-specific twist.”

“Yes.”

“Or whether the two threads respond identically to the same disturbance.”

“Yes.”

“So it is a bad control.”

“No.”

I frowned.

“It is an incomplete control.”

“That sounds like a polite bad control.”

“It is a control for some questions and not others.”

Of course. Everything with Hessa eventually became jurisdiction. Even thread.

“You are angry.”

“No.”

“You are disappointed.”

“Yes.”

“Better.”

“I would prefer established external effect.”

“I would prefer a patient who does not build conclusions out of wishes.”

“I did not.”

“You almost did.”

“That is different.”

“Barely.”

She covered the apparatus with the gray cloth. I objected.

“With my face?”

“With your entire body.”

“You said the test was more interpretable.”

“Yes.”

“Then repeat it.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“One supervised external attempt today.”

“You did not say one before.”

“I am saying it now.”

“That is cheating.”

“I am the doctor.”

“You use that too much.”

“I use it exactly enough.”

She returned to the desk. I sat. My forearm felt normal. Which was good. Boring. Good.

“Hessa.”

“No.”

“I have not asked.”

“You want to know when.”

“Yes.”

“I don't know.”

“Tomorrow?”

“No magic tomorrow.”

I stared.

“One day?”

“One day.”

“Then?”

“Assessment.”

“External?”

“Assessment.”

“You are doing that deliberately.”

“Yes.”

I thought about arguing. I did not. Not wisdom. I had already lost. She wrote.

“Thirteenth successful minimal supervised draw.”

There was the count.

“Ninth supervised deliberate shaping attempt?”

“Yes.”

“Second supervised external attempt?”

“Yes.”

“External effect?”

“Unestablished.”

I hated the word. It was correct.

“Internal control?”

“Still encouraging.”

“Encouraging.”

“Yes.”

“Not improved?”

She looked up.

“You established a small altered region at a shifted target, attempted one bounded REACH, RETURNed promptly, maintained the underlying draw, and showed no motor recruitment, broadening, thumb symptom, elbowward shift, or unusual left response.”

“Yes.”

“That supports repeatability of the control sequence under a slightly changed setup.”

“Yes.”

“That is improvement in confidence.”

“Not effect.”

“Correct.”

“Fine.”

“You sound like you are trying to punish the word.”

“I am.”

“Tomorrow you live.”

“I have been doing that.”

“Continue.”

“What exactly are you protecting against now?”

She considered me for a moment. Not because she did not know. Because she was deciding how much to say.

“Accumulation.”

“Of what?”

“Unknowns.”

“That is not a symptom.”

“No. It is why I do not stack tests.”

She pointed at my right forearm.

“You have had repeated small draws, repeated shaping, a new external instruction, and now a second external attempt. Your immediate exams are reassuring. That does not mean I know every delayed cost.”

“There hasn't been one.”

“So far.”

“Yes.”

“Good. Keep helping me preserve that sentence.”

I did not like this either. It was difficult to argue against a strategy whose main evidence was that nothing bad had happened.

“You could just say you are cautious.”

“I have.”

“Many times.”

“And yet.”

Fine. She gave me ten minutes. No magic. Ordinary hand movement. Cup. Grip. Crutch. She watched me pick up the cup.

“Stop checking your thumb.”

“I wasn't.”

“You checked.”

“I moved it.”

“You checked by moving it.”

“That is how thumbs work.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

At the door she said:

“Do not buy thread.”

I stopped.

“I own thread.”

“Do not hang it from anything.”

“I was not going to.”

“Do not ask the theatre for theirs.”

I stared at her.

“How do you know about theatre thread?”

“I know about thread.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“Go live.”

I went. The morning had become late enough that the Guild was busy. I did not have a reason to go there. I went anyway. Jorren was eating an apple on the front steps.

Of course. He looked at me.

“Hessa?”

“Yes.”

“Alive?”

“Yes.”

“Boring.”

I sat beside him. Not gracefully. He did not help. Correct. He took another bite.

“What happened?”

“Nothing established.”

“That sounds expensive.”

“It was free.”

“Then you got your money's worth.”

“No.”

“No?”

“I got one movement.”

“You said nothing established.”

“Correct.”

“Then you got one unestablished movement.”

“That is not a thing.”

“It is clearly a thing. You have one.”

I looked at him. He bit the apple again.

“What did the other movement do?”

I stopped.

“What?”

“You said one movement.”

“I did not say there were two threads.”

“There were two threads?”

“Yes.”

“Then this story is already too complicated.”

“It is not complicated.”

“There are twice as many threads as yesterday.”

“Two days ago.”

“Worse.”

I almost explained the control. He held up the apple.

“No.”

“You asked.”

“I regret it.”

“You cannot ask a technical question and then refuse the answer.”

“I just did.”

“That is socially irresponsible.”

“Eat something.”

I looked at him. He offered the apple. I took it. One bite. Returned it. He frowned.

“You eat like a thief.”

“You offered.”

“I offered generosity. You took geometry.”

“What?”

“That bite was too large.”

“No.”

“It changed the apple.”

“That is what biting does.”

He inspected the missing section.

“Damage.”

I almost explained the two-thread control. Did not. Not because Jorren would not understand. Because I did not want to. I wanted lunch.

“Are you working?” I asked.

“Later.”

“What?”

“Warehouse.”

“Which?”

He looked at me.

“No.”

“Fine.”

He smiled. Good. We sat. People went into Guild. People came out.

Merrin passed carrying three ledgers and said:

“Gregory.”

“Merrin.”

No offer. No task. Good. A courier I did not know argued with a clerk about a damaged seal. A woman in a red coat shouted that somebody had moved her cart. Someone had.

The cart was across the street. The argument continued anyway. Jorren finished the apple.

“You going theatre?”

“I don't know.”

“Lyssa?”

“I don't know.”

“Pessa?”

“I don't know.”

“You have a demanding schedule.”

“Yes.”

“What are you doing now?”

“Lunch.”

“You don't have lunch.”

“I am about to.”

“That is not lunch.”

“It will become lunch.”

He stood.

“I have work.”

“Later.”

“Later became now.”

I looked at the sun.

“That is poor scheduling.”

“That is time.”

He left. No theft. Unusual. I bought stew. Sat near the Guild wall. A cart passed. Then another. No ancient beast. No dangerous authority. No impossible old-world recognition. Just Carrow. I ate. The thread entered my head after three bites.

Near moved. Far did not. Then later far moved. Could be mana. Could be room. Could be me. Could be nothing. I wanted another test. Tomorrow contained no magic. Fine. The theatre was west.

Lyssa might be anywhere. Pessa might be busy. Work existed. I finished the stew. For once, I did not decide what the rest of the day meant. I stood. Then waited because my right crutch tip had landed on a cabbage leaf.

I moved it six inches. Better. Current state. Continue.
CHAPTER 126
THE OLD HAND

No magic. Again. This was becoming a profession. I woke with both hands normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present. No thumb. No fingers. No Hessa until tomorrow. Fine. The yellow bird was still on the table.

I had started noticing that every morning. That was probably how objects became furniture. I ate. The keeper looked at my shirt. Brown. She opened her mouth.

“No.”

She closed it. Victory. Outside, Carrow was wet. Not raining. Recently raining. The stones held it. Crutch tips disliked that. I went slower. No destination yet. That was becoming less alarming too. At the Guild, a cart was blocking half the front.

Not Guild cart. Courier cart. Long bed. High rear wheel. Canvas rolled along one side. A man was under it. Boots only. I knew the boots.

“Sevren.”

From beneath the cart:

“No.”

“You are under your cart.”

“No.”

“Your boots are visible.”

“That proves nothing.”

I waited. He slid out. Sevren had grease on one cheek.

“That is unfortunate.”

“You found me.”

“Yes.”

“Go away.”

“No.”

He sat up.

“Why?”

“I don't know.”

“Good reason.”

He looked at my crutches. Then at the wet street.

“You walk here?”

“Yes.”

“Bad road.”

“This is a street.”

“Bad street.”

He stood. The cart wheel had its outer cap removed. A pin lay on a folded rag.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why is it apart?”

“Because I prefer fixing things before the part where something happens.”

Reasonable. Annoying.

“You doing the north run?”

He looked at me.

“Eventually.”

“That is not a date.”

“No.”

“You said next week.”

“I say many things.”

“That was more than a week ago.”

“Then I lied.”

“You did not know.”

“Same result.”

Not same. I let it go. Mostly. He crouched again. I watched. He reseated the pin. Tapped it. Turned the wheel. Stopped. Tapped again.

“You changed the route?”

He looked up.

“Why?”

“You said route wasn't final.”

“It still isn't.”

“That seems inefficient.”

“That is roads.”

I considered this.

“What changed?”

“Bridge.”

“Which?”

“The north bridge.”

“There are several.”

“The one you mean.”

That was offensive.

“The stone bridge after the second rise?”

“No.”

“The timber bridge before the toll house?”

He paused.

“What toll house?”

I looked at him.

“The toll house.”

“What toll house?”

“North road. Before the old timber bridge. Gray roof. Two gates. Used to charge freight by axle width.”

Sevren stared.

“Used to?”

“Yes.”

“How old are you?”

“Fuck you.”

He laughed. Good.

Then:

“There hasn't been a toll house there since before I started running north.”

I stopped. No. That could mean several things.

“When did you start?”

“Years.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“That is not useful.”

“It burned.”

“The toll house?”

“Apparently.”

“When?”

“Before me.”

I looked at the cart. Then north. Not actually visible. Memory arrived. Gray roof. Two gates. Man with one ear. Freight line. Old Greg waiting behind a wagon loaded with iron pipe.

The clerk measuring axle width with a marked stick because somebody had tried to file down the outer rims. Real. Clear. Not recent. Of course.

“What replaced it?”

“Nothing.”

“That bridge still charges.”

“No.”

“It did.”

“Apparently.”

“Then who maintains it?”

Sevren wiped grease from his fingers.

“Not the same people who used to.”

“Who?”

“Depends which bridge you mean.”

“The timber bridge.”

“Gone.”

I looked at him.

“Gone?”

“Flood.”

“When?”

“Three winters ago.”

That was worse.

“What replaced it?”

“Stone crossing lower down.”

I knew the lower crossing. Bad grade. Narrow. Soft shoulder in rain.

“You don't take freight there.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“The turn is too tight for a long cart.”

“Was.”

“What does that mean?”

“They cut the bank.”

I hated everything. Sevren watched me.

“You know this road?”

“I knew this road.”

There. Different sentence. He nodded as though this explained more than it did.

“Come look.”

He pulled a folded route sheet from the cart box. Not a map. List. Stops. Distances. Notes. Marks. He held it low enough for me to see. North gate. First rise. Old quarry fork.

Lower stone crossing. Second village. Return east spur. I recognized enough to be dangerous. Not literally. Probably.

“That fork doesn't save time.”

“It does now.”

“No. The quarry road narrows after the cut.”

“Quarry expanded.”

“What?”

“They widened the road.”

“Why?”

“Quarry.”

“That is circular.”

“It is a quarry road.”

I looked again. There was another notation.

“East spur?”

“New grading.”

“That used to wash out.”

“Still does.”

“So why?”

“Faster when dry.”

“It rained.”

“Here.”

He pointed north with his chin.

“Didn't there.”

I looked at the sky. This was useless. Weather had geography. Known problem. Still irritating.

“You carrying two villages?”

“Three now.”

“You said two.”

“Third added.”

“Why?”

“Because they pay.”

I stared at the sheet.

“Who?”

“No.”

“I meant who added it.”

“Same answer.”

Professional boundary. Fine.

“What are you carrying?”

“No.”

“Weight?”

He looked at me.

“Why?”

“Because I am asking whether the lower crossing is sensible.”

“No, you're trying to solve my route.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is exactly the same thing.”

I sat on the cart edge. Carefully.

“Your rear axle load matters.”

“Yes.”

“The lower crossing used to pitch left after rain.”

“Used to.”

I hated that word. Sevren smiled.

“You keep saying things like a dead surveyor.”

I went still. Not because he knew. He did not. He was making fun of me.

“That's rude.”

“Accurate?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He went back under the cart. I kept looking at the route sheet in his hand. He had not taken it away. That meant I could read it. Probably.

“Your return is longer.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Bridge.”

“Which bridge?”

He laughed from under the cart.

“Now you care.”

“I always cared.”

“That's the problem.”

I waited. He slid out again.

“North bridge has one-way freight hours now.”

“What?”

“Carters east in the morning, west in afternoon.”

“Why?”

“Too narrow after reinforcement.”

“They reinforced it by making it worse?”

“They reinforced it by keeping it standing.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“Roads don't care.”

I knew the bridge. Old Greg knew it. Wide enough for two carts if both drivers were not idiots. Apparently not anymore.

“What happened?”

“Central support cracked two years ago. They braced it. Lost width.”

“And nobody replaced it?”

“Somebody plans to.”

“Who?”

“People who plan bridges.”

“That is not a profession.”

“It absolutely is.”

I looked at him. He looked at me. Fine.

“Why not use lower crossing both ways?”

“Third village.”

“Right.”

New stop changed return geometry. Of course. I could still solve it. No. I could solve a route from information Sevren had and I did not. Different. He took the route sheet back.

“Done?”

“With what?”

“Trying to make my road older.”

“That is not what I was doing.”

“You were arguing with three years ago.”

“That bridge existed.”

“I believe you.”

“I used it.”

He looked at me. Small pause. Too small for alarm.

“You've been north?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Long time ago.”

“How long?”

I looked at him. He looked back. There were answers. None good.

“I don't remember exactly.”

That was true enough. He accepted it. Or did not care. Better. He folded the sheet.

“Anyway.”

“Anyway?”

“You asked about the run.”

“Yes.”

“Route isn't final.”

“That is now obvious.”

“Third stop might drop.”

“Why?”

“Buyer arguing price.”

“What are you carrying?”

“No.”

“Fine.”

He put the sheet away. I thought that was the end.

Then he said:

“You want a day?”

“What?”

“North.”

I stared. He pointed at the passenger board beside the driver's bench. Not a seat. A narrow plank. I knew this cart from the west-market run. Different load. Different distance.

“Doing what?”

“Nothing yet.”

“Then that is not work.”

“Correct.”

“You are asking if I want to ride.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you keep asking about the road.”

“That is not a reason.”

“It is mine.”

I looked at the cart. Long run. Two villages becoming three. Route not final. Passenger plank. Crutches. Body. Stairs irrelevant. Road vibration very relevant.

“What day?”

“Don't know.”

“That matters.”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Full day if two stops. Longer if three.”

“That also matters.”

“Yes.”

“Can I get off?”

He stared.

“At villages.”

“Along route?”

“If needed.”

“Roadside?”

“Yes.”

“Can the crutches ride secured?”

“Yes.”

“Is there space?”

“Depends load.”

“So you don't know.”

“No.”

“Then you are not offering.”

“I am asking if you want me to consider you when I know.”

That was different. I looked at the passenger board again. The west-market run had been bounded. Shorter. Known. This would not be. A full day on a cart meant sitting differently than a chair.

Road vibration. Getting down at stops. Getting back up. Bathroom. Food. Rain. Crutches secured somewhere they would not become freight. The list arrived without permission. Sevren watched me make it.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You're counting problems.”

“Yes.”

“Useful?”

“Some.”

“Which?”

“Whether I can get off the cart without making you lift me.”

“I am not lifting you.”

“Good.”

“You got off last time.”

“Different cart loading.”

“Same cart.”

“Different cargo.”

He looked behind him. The bed was mostly empty now.

“That changes where I can brace.”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

“Also if the passenger board stays clear.”

“Yes.”

“And whether there is room to secure both crutches where I can reach them.”

“Yes.”

“And road duration.”

“Yes.”

“And stops.”

“Yes.”

“And whether you expect me to jump down if something happens.”

“No.”

“Good.”

“You cannot jump.”

“I can fall aggressively.”

“That is not a service I need.”

“Then we agree.”

He pointed at the cart bed.

“If the load leaves no room, you don't come.”

“Fine.”

“If the road turns worse than expected, I decide whether we continue.”

“That depends.”

“No.”

“Hessa owns medicine.”

“I own cart.”

I stared at him. Fair. Annoying.

“If you decide road conditions make the cart unsafe, yes.”

“That is what I said.”

“It was not precise.”

“It was enough.”

I disliked how often that word had started appearing around me. Not connected. Probably.

“Yes.”

He nodded. No ceremony.

“Good.”

“What would I be doing?”

“Maybe nothing.”

“That is unacceptable.”

“Then no.”

“I mean if I come.”

“Could check receipts. Could hold route sheet. Could sit and complain about bridges.”

“I can do two of those professionally.”

“Which two?”

“No.”

He grinned. Then the Guild clerk called his name. Sevren stood.

“Need seal.”

“For the run?”

“No.”

Different work. Of course. He went inside. I stayed with the cart. Not guarding it. Probably. A woman walked around it and swore because one wheel occupied the gutter. A boy tried to touch the exposed wheel cap.

I said:

“Don't.”

He did anyway. Nothing happened. Good. Sevren returned with a waxed packet.

“That's not a seal.”

“It contains one.”

“Why?”

“No.”

Fine. He put it in the cart box.

“What now?”

“South warehouse.”

“You just said north.”

“Later.”

“This is a different job.”

“Yes.”

“How many jobs do you have?”

“Enough.”

I almost went with him. Not because invited. Because cart. Road. Movement. No. I had no reason.

“Tell me when the north route is real.”

“I will if I need you.”

“That is not what I said.”

“It is what I mean.”

He climbed onto the driver's bench. Then looked down.

“Greg.”

“Yes?”

“The toll house.”

“Yes.”

“Where exactly?”

I told him. Gray roof. Before timber bridge. Two gates. Axle measuring stick. Old freight yard behind it. He frowned.

“There are foundation stones there.”

I stopped.

“What?”

“Past the willow bend. Low wall. I thought old weigh station.”

“It was toll.”

“Maybe.”

“It was.”

“Fine.”

He considered.

“Gray roof?”

“Yes.”

“Slate?”

“No. Wood shingle. Dark.”

He nodded.

“Interesting.”

That was all. Not impossible. Not terrifying. Just something I knew that had become stones beside a road. Then he left. The cart rolled south. I sat on the Guild step. Merrin came out.

“You waiting for work?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“That sounded hostile.”

“It sounded efficient.”

He carried a stack of receipts. I looked. He moved them away.

“No.”

“I did not ask.”

“You leaned.”

Everyone had learned Lyssa's method.

“I can work.”

“I know.”

“Do you have anything?”

“Yes.”

“Suitable?”

“Probably.”

“Duration?”

“Forty minutes.”

“Seated?”

“Yes.”

I considered. I wanted something ordinary after losing an argument with a bridge.

“Yes.”

He handed me half the stack.

“Compare dates and totals. Flag mismatches. Do not fix.”

“I know.”

“I know you know.”

That was satisfying. I worked. Forty minutes became fifty because one receipt had been copied badly. I flagged it. Did not fix. Merrin paid me the agreed small amount. No exact purse theory. Good.

Before I left, I asked:

“Do courier route sheets get filed here?”

“Some.”

“Old ones?”

“Sometimes.”

“How old?”

He looked at me.

“No.”

“I am asking generally.”

“You never ask generally.”

“That is becoming slander.”

“Why?”

“North road.”

“Ask Sevren.”

“I did.”

“Then why are you asking me?”

Because I wanted to know whether a piece of paper somewhere could prove the road I remembered had existed exactly the way I remembered it. That was not useful. Not today.

“Never mind.”

Merrin nodded as though I had finally answered correctly. At lunch I thought about the toll house. Not nostalgically. Mostly. Old Greg had known it accurately. Gray roof. Two gates. One-eared collector. Axle-width charge.

All real.

Now:

burned. Bridge gone. Lower crossing widened. Quarry expanded. New bridge restrictions. Third village added. Same road. Different road.

I could have argued every old detail correctly and still sent a cart into a route that no longer existed. That was unpleasant. Also obvious. People had not frozen. Roads had not frozen. I knew that.

Knowing something generally and discovering it specifically were different annoyances. I ate. No magic. Tomorrow Hessa. The near thread moved. The far did not. No. Road. I pulled my notebook out. Stopped. What was I going to write?

TOLL HOUSE BURNED? Useful if traveling. BRIDGE GONE? Definitely useful. LOWER CROSSING WIDENED? Maybe. I wrote three lines. Not a theory. Just road facts.

Then added:

ASK CURRENT ROUTE. I stared at that. Too much like a rule. I almost scratched it out. Did not. Because if I went north, asking the current route was simply intelligent. No philosophical consequence required.

I closed the notebook. On the way home, I passed a wagon whose driver was arguing that a street had always been one-way. Another driver said it changed last month. Neither moved. Current intelligence did not guarantee intelligence either.

Good. The keeper was sweeping the entry when I returned.

“Brown.”

“No.”

“Theatre?”

“No.”

“Guild?”

“Partly.”

She thought.

“Courier?”

“Maybe.”

She lowered the broom.

“That is too many categories.”

“Yes.”

Finally. Upstairs, the yellow bird was still on the table. The world had moved around it all day. It had managed not to care. Tomorrow Hessa. Tonight, no magic. I lay down. For several minutes I tried to remember the old north bridge exactly.

I could remember the toll collector's missing ear. I could remember the axle stick. I could remember the smell of wet rope. I could not remember whether the bridge rails had been painted. This offended me less than it once would have.

The bridge was gone anyway.
CHAPTER 127
THE REPEATER

Hessa had the same two threads. I checked. Same frame. Same glazed tile. Same copper. Same dark thread. Same spacing. Probably. I looked closer.

Hessa said:

“Sit down.”

“I am checking whether you changed it.”

“I changed one thing.”

I stopped.

“What?”

“Sit.”

I sat. She checked me first. Hands. Right calf. Residual limb. Phantom. Thumb. Fingers. Wrist. Grip. No surprises. The phantom foot was mildly cold despite not existing. Ordinary. Hessa pressed along my right forearm.

“Yesterday?”

“No magic.”

“Thread?”

“No.”

“String?”

“No.”

“Cord?”

“No.”

I looked at her.

“You are expanding the prohibition.”

“You went to Guild.”

“Yes.”

“Courier?”

“Yes.”

“Did you tie anything to anything?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“That question is absurd.”

“You are creative when annoyed.”

“I repaired a horse with wood.”

“Not yesterday.”

“No.”

“Good.”

She went to the apparatus.

“What changed?”

She pointed at the two threads. Small paper sleeves covered the upper inch of each. One white. One gray.

“That.”

“Why?”

“So I stop thinking of them as near and far while I record.”

I stared.

“You know which is which.”

“Yes.”

“That does not work.”

“It helps.”

“How?”

“It makes me write white and gray instead of the conclusion I expect.”

“That is not blinding.”

“No.”

“Barely even pretending.”

“Yes.”

“Then why?”

“Because perfect is not available.”

She moved the frame. Not far. Half an inch. Then put it back against two charcoal marks on the table. I noticed those too.

“You marked the feet.”

“Yes.”

“To preserve position.”

“Yes.”

“That is a second change.”

“The marks were there last time.”

I looked. They were faint. I had missed them. Annoying. Hessa adjusted the tile.

“Question today is replication.”

I liked the word. She saw that.

“Do not.”

“I did nothing.”

“You liked it.”

“Yes.”

“Stop.”

“No.”

She ignored me.

“Same bounded sequence. Same target region. Same approximate geometry. Same near comparison and farther comparison. One attempt.”

“Same charcoal mark?”

“Re-drawn from my notes.”

“So not exactly.”

“No.”

“Same thread?”

“Yes.”

“Same cup?”

“What cup?”

“Nothing.”

She looked at me. I looked back. Horse stayed out of this room. Good.

“What counts as replication?” I asked.

“Nothing by itself.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the answer you need.”

“Hessa.”

“If the closer thread again shows a movement toward your arm during REACH while the farther thread does not at the same time, that would be another observation of the same general pattern.”

“Yes.”

“If it does not, that is also information.”

“Yes.”

“If both move together, information.”

“Yes.”

“If the farther moves and the closer does not, information.”

“Yes.”

“If neither moves, information.”

“Yes.”

“So everything is information.”

“Correct.”

“That is convenient.”

“It is only convenient if you do not care what the information says.”

I did. Obviously. She opened the door. Waited. Both threads moved. White more. Gray less. She wrote. Closed door. Waited. Neither. She walked past the table. Gray trembled. White did not. She wrote. Opened the window a finger width.

Both moved left. Not together. White first. Gray second. She wrote. Closed it. We waited. The room settled. Mostly. Hessa moved my chair into position. Right forearm beside the closer thread. I could tell which sleeve was closer.

White. So could Hessa. This was not blinding. Still. She had changed how she wrote. Maybe that mattered. I breathed normally. White moved slightly away from me. Gray rotated. Hessa wrote. White returned near its line.

Gray stopped left of its line.

“Baseline is worse today,” I said.

“Different.”

“More movement.”

“So far.”

“Humidity?”

“Maybe.”

“Wet yesterday.”

“Outside.”

“Could affect room.”

“Yes.”

“Thread moisture.”

“Yes.”

“Air.”

“Yes.”

“Heat.”

“Yes.”

“Static less likely if damp.”

“Less likely is not absent.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

I wanted to ask how long we were going to watch thread before doing anything. I did not. Five minutes. Maybe six. Long enough that my right shoulder became aware of the chair. Not pain.

Position. Hessa moved the chair back.

“Reset.”

“What?”

“You shifted.”

“I breathed.”

“You also leaned.”

“I did not.”

“You did.”

“How much?”

“Enough that I noticed.”

“That is not measurement.”

“No.”

She made me stand. I did. She reset the chair against a floor mark I had not noticed. Of course there was a floor mark. I sat again.

“Do not hold yourself rigid.”

“I wasn't.”

“You are now.”

“Because you said I moved.”

“Normal posture.”

“That is impossible after instruction.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

I tried to forget my spine. Failed. Eventually succeeded enough. Hessa waited another two minutes.

“Draw.”

Minimal. Right forearm. Copper answered. Small. Stable. No thumb. No finger. No wrist. No left response.

“Shape.”

Same region. Or as close to same as memory and charcoal allowed. Localized alteration. Near edge slightly more distinct. Upper edge faint. Center changed. I reported each.

“Hold.”

Held. White thread moved. Small. Away from my arm. I saw it. Hessa had not told me to look away yet. My chest sank. Interesting. Disappointing. Useful. Probably. Gray moved a moment later. Toward the window.

Hessa wrote.

“That was during shape,” she said.

“I know.”

“Keep it there.”

“REACH.”

I looked at her hand. Two fingers above copper. Same as last time. Smallest extension. Toward the closer thread. No force. No push. Maintain draw. The near edge sharpened. Asymmetry toward target. Familiar now.

Not comfortable. Familiar.

“Near edge sharper.”

“Continue same instruction.”

I did. Nothing else internally. No broadening. No motor. No urge. No thumb. Hessa watched past me. I watched her fingers. One breath. Two. Three.

“Hold.”

Held.

“RETURN.”

I returned. Altered region softened. Center diminished. Upper edge faded. Underlying draw stayed.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Release.”

Released. Hessa was at my wrist immediately. Open. Close. Thumb. Wrist. Grip. Again. Fine. She checked the forearm. Then the left. Then made me wait. I looked at the threads. White rested almost on its charcoal line.

Gray sat a little right.

“What happened?”

Hessa wrote first. That was cruel.

“Hessa.”

“White moved during shape.”

“I saw.”

“Away from your arm.”

“Yes.”

“Gray moved shortly after.”

“Yes.”

“During REACH?”

I waited. She finished the line.

“Neither moved enough for me to mark.”

I stared.

“Neither.”

“Correct.”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing I recorded.”

“During the entire REACH?”

“Yes.”

“White didn't move toward me.”

“No.”

“Gray?”

“No.”

“So it did not replicate.”

“The specific differential movement from last time did not replicate today.”

There was the sentence. I disliked it. It was clean.

“Could still have been mana last time.”

“Yes.”

“Could be mana today without movement.”

“That question is not useful.”

“It is possible.”

“Many things are possible.”

“Could the shape have changed the thread during the movement away?”

“You had not begun REACH.”

“I was shaping.”

“Yes.”

“That is still mana.”

“Yes.”

I looked at her. She raised one finger.

“No.”

“You cannot just exclude it.”

“I am not excluding it.”

“You are.”

“I am refusing to move the question because today's answer disappointed you.”

I stopped. That landed. I hated when she did that.

“The test was REACH.”

“Yes.”

“The movement during shape was not the target observation.”

“Correct.”

“But it happened.”

“Yes.”

“And could matter.”

“Yes.”

“Then record it.”

“I did.”

Fine.

“What does it mean?”

“I don't know.”

“Useful.”

“Yes.”

“You use that phrase badly.”

“I use it accurately.”

She sat. I remained in the test chair.

“Last time,” she said, “closer thread moved toward your arm during REACH while farther did not at that moment.”

“Yes.”

“Today, it did not.”

“Yes.”

“That lowers my confidence that we are seeing a repeatable external response under this setup.”

There. Actual movement. Down. Not up. I did not like it. I also trusted it more because I did not like it. Probably dangerous thought.

“What about internal control?”

“Still good.”

“Same?”

“Good.”

“That is not a number.”

“No.”

“Better confidence?”

She looked at her notes.

“Fourteenth successful minimal supervised draw.”

I waited.

“Tenth supervised shaping attempt.”

“Yes.”

“Third supervised external attempt.”

“Yes.”

“You established the localized alteration at the intended shifted region.”

“Yes.”

“You maintained underlying draw.”

“Yes.”

“You attempted one bounded REACH without broadening, force sensation, motor recruitment, thumb symptom, wrist movement, elbowward shift, or unusual left response.”

“Yes.”

“You RETURNed promptly.”

“Yes.”

“So yes. My confidence in that sequence increases again.”

I nodded. External down. Internal up. Annoying. Balanced. Probably.

“What next?”

“No magic tomorrow.”

I closed my eyes.

“One day.”

“Yes.”

“Then assessment?”

“Yes.”

“External?”

“Assessment.”

“You enjoy that.”

“A little.”

I opened my eyes.

“Are you going to use the same threads again?”

“I don't know.”

“You must have a plan.”

“I have several.”

“Which?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to decide after I review all three attempts, not while you are sitting here trying to make one of them win.”

“I am not trying to make it win.”

“You are arguing that movement during shape should count.”

“It should be recorded.”

“It was.”

“Then yes.”

She almost smiled.

“Good.”

I looked at the white sleeve.

“Why keep the paper labels if you know which is near?”

“Because I noticed something in my own notes.”

“What?”

“I wrote ‘near moved’ more quickly than I wrote the actual direction.”

I looked at her.

“That is bad.”

“Yes.”

“You are admitting error.”

“Yes.”

“Are you ill?”

“No.”

“Should I check your grip?”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

She tapped the page.

“Near is already interpretation. White is an object.”

“That seems excessive.”

“Probably.”

“Then why do it?”

“Cheap.”

I had no answer. She won. Again. I pointed at the gray cloth.

“Are you changing the apparatus next time?”

“I said I don't know.”

“The comparison is imperfect.”

“Yes.”

“Local heat differs.”

“Yes.”

“Distance differs.”

“Yes.”

“Air around my arm differs.”

“Yes.”

“Thread behavior differs.”

“Yes.”

“So improve it.”

“How?”

“Put a second target at the same distance from another part of me.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because then you are changing what you are doing internally.”

“Not necessarily.”

“Yes.”

“I could shape two regions.”

“No.”

“Not simultaneously.”

“No.”

“Separate trials.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I am not doubling your shaping to improve my thread experiment.”

That was irritatingly reasonable.

“Then use a barrier between the threads.”

“That changes airflow.”

“Shield both.”

“Changes the room.”

“Enclose the frame.”

“Heat.”

“Larger enclosure.”

“Greg.”

“Yes.”

“You are trying to design the perfect apparatus.”

“Yes.”

“There isn't one.”

“There can be a better one.”

“Yes.”

“Then why not?”

“Because better for one confound can be worse for another, and because I also care whether the same simple setup ever gives the same result twice.”

I looked at the covered frame.

“That is why you repeated it unchanged.”

“Mostly unchanged.”

“Paper sleeves.”

“Those are for me.”

“Still changed.”

“Yes.”

“You hate that.”

“Yes.”

Good. At least the universe remained stable.

“What if the next test is different?”

“Then I will tell you the question before you do anything.”

“And if it is the same?”

“Same.”

“One attempt?”

“Probably.”

“No magic after?”

“Depends.”

“Hessa.”

“Assessment.”

I hated that word almost as much as unestablished. She gathered the copper and set it beside her notes. I noticed three pages. One for each external attempt. The first page had more writing than the other two.

Of course it did. Messier question. Messier notes.

“What are you looking for when you review?”

“Patterns.”

“That is vague.”

“Symptoms first.”

“None.”

“So far.”

“Then control sequence.”

“Yes.”

“Then apparatus behavior before, during, after.”

“Yes.”

“Then whether anything I thought mattered was actually just memorable.”

I stopped.

“What?”

She tapped the first page.

“Two movements are memorable.”

“Yes.”

“Memorable is not the same as diagnostic.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

The second page.

“One differential movement is memorable.”

“Yes.”

“The third page refusing to repeat it is also memorable.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She stacked them.

“That is why I am reviewing all three.”

Not to decide which story she liked. Fine. I understood. Still wanted the thread to move. Hessa covered the frame. Gray cloth. Threads gone.

“No magic tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

“No thread.”

“Yes.”

“No hanging cord.”

“Yes.”

“No clever substitutes.”

“I am not going to move dust.”

She stared.

“I was making a joke.”

“Do not move dust.”

“Hessa.”

“Go.”

I went. Outside, I stood for a moment. The result should have disappointed me more. It did disappoint me. I wanted the thread to move. Again. Same direction. Same timing. I wanted a clean line through three observations and a conclusion at the end.

Instead:

First test ambiguous. Second test suggestive. Third test did not repeat the suggestive part. That was not failure. It was not success. It was science being an asshole. I walked. Not Guild. Not theatre.

Not Lyssa. At the first corner I nearly turned toward Hessa again. Not to argue. To ask one more question. Different problem. Same behavior. I kept going. A baker had set two trays near the open window.

One sweet. One not. I could smell the sweet one from across the street. That was enough information to make me cross. No. Stop. I bought a pear instead because I had already committed to not turning lunch into a system.

The pear seller gave me the softer of two without asking. I noticed.

“Why that one?”

“You'll eat it now.”

“How do you know?”

“You're holding it.”

“That happened after you chose it.”

She looked at me.

“Do you want the hard one?”

“No.”

“Then go away.”

I went away. Carrow remained hostile to inquiry. I bought a pear. Sat on a low wall. A dog stared at me. I stared back. The dog looked away first. Established external effect. No.

I ate the pear. A cart went past. Not Sevren. A woman carrying flowers stopped to retie one bundle. Two boys argued about whether a roof tile had fallen today or yesterday. Nobody knew.

The dog came back. Sat near my right crutch. Brown. One white paw. Its left ear folded at the tip. It watched my pear with professional attention. I shifted the core from my right hand to my left.

Its eyes followed. That was an external effect. No. That was a dog. I did not test anything on it. Good. I put the pear core on the wall beside me instead. The dog looked at it.

Then at me. Then at it. This was already a better experiment than thread because the dog clearly wanted something. Also worse because dogs had opinions. It stood. Took one step toward the wall.

Stopped. I did nothing. The dog sat again.

“Your controls are terrible,” I told it.

Its tail moved once. Could be wind. I laughed before I could stop myself. A man passing with a sack looked at me.

“Dog won't eat pear.”

“I can see that.”

“He'll eat sausage.”

“I don't have sausage.”

“Then you've designed badly.”

He kept walking. I stared after him. Everyone in Carrow had become Hessa. Unacceptable. My forearm felt normal. Hands normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom toes appeared briefly when I shifted. Ordinary. Tomorrow no magic.

Fine. I finished the pear. The dog watched the core. I held it out. It sniffed. Did not take it. Non-replication.

“Fuck you too.”

The dog left. I laughed. Then went home.
CHAPTER 128
THE MESSENGER

I went to the theatre because I wanted to. This was becoming suspicious. No Hessa. No magic. No Guild task. No courier cart. The theatre door was open.

Inside, somebody was shouting:

“Not the blue one.”

A different voice shouted:

“They are both blue.”

“Not that blue one.”

I entered. Two painted doors stood onstage. Both blue. One darker. Probably. The soot-shirt worker was carrying a brass handle in her teeth. She saw me. Pointed at the darker door. Then pointed at the floor beside it.

I went there.

“What?”

She removed the handle.

“Hold this.”

She gave me the door. Not metaphorically. It was lighter than it looked. Canvas over frame. I braced it with one hand while keeping a crutch under the other arm. Bad arrangement. She looked.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

She took the door back.

“Sit.”

There was a chair near the stage edge. I sat. She put the door beside me.

“Hold from there.”

Better.

“Why?”

“Because I need the hinge.”

“Which hinge?”

“The one you are covering.”

I moved my hand. She took the hinge.

“Excellent.”

“That was not useful.”

“It was eventually.”

Good morning. Teren was at his usual place with pages. He looked up.

“Gregory.”

“Teren.”

“Can you read?”

“Yes.”

“Today?”

“Probably.”

He held out three folded pages. I took them.

“What am I?”

“Messenger.”

I looked at the page. The title at the top was not the play title. Just scene number and a word I did not know. I pointed.

“What is that?”

“Scene change note.”

“It looks like a name.”

“It isn't.”

“What does it mean?”

“Blue room after court.”

“That is four words.”

“It saves space.”

“It failed.”

“For you.”

“Then it failed.”

Teren took the page back, looked at the note, and said:

“No.”

He gave it back.

The servant actor called from the floor:

“Gregory has discovered notation.”

“I can read notation.”

“Today?”

“Fuck you.”

The woman said:

“Please keep him. He improves morale.”

Teren said:

“He is not mine.”

Good. Correct. I looked at the page again. There was a messenger. Four lines.

“No.”

Teren blinked.

“What?”

“I mean what am I doing?”

“Reading messenger.”

“That sounds like what I am.”

“For six minutes.”

“Why?”

“Because we are working the entrance.”

I looked toward the stage. The recurring woman was there in a dark skirt over rehearsal clothes. The servant actor was lying on the floor. Not dead. Probably. Another man stood by the blue door.

Actual actors. No missing person. No emergency. Teren pointed.

“You enter from there.”

He pointed to the darker blue door.

“Walk to the table.”

There was no table.

“There is no table.”

“There will be.”

“Where?”

The woman pointed at a chalk rectangle on the floor.

“There.”

“Why not put the table there?”

“Because they're painting it.”

Reasonable. I looked at the page. Messenger entered. Crossed to table. Delivered letter. Four lines. Exited.

“Why me?”

Teren had already looked back at his pages.

“Because you are here.”

That answer was becoming dangerous. The servant actor sat up.

“Gregory has been promoted.”

“To what?”

“Temporary furniture.”

“I am messenger.”

“Temporary messenger furniture.”

The woman said:

“Start before he develops standards.”

I stood. Crutches. Pages. Letter. Too many things. Teren noticed.

“Pages stay with me.”

Good. He took them back.

“You know the lines?”

“No.”

“You just read them.”

“That is not the same thing.”

He held them where I could see. Fine. The letter was a folded scrap. I tucked it under two fingers on my right crutch handle.

Teren said:

“No.”

Everyone said no here.

“What?”

“You need to hand it over.”

“Yes.”

“You have trapped it.”

I looked. True.

“Pocket.”

I put it in my shirt pocket.

The woman onstage said:

“Messenger does not arrive with royal correspondence folded into his armpit.”

“It is my pocket.”

“Worse.”

“Why?”

“Because then I watch you dig for it.”

“You are supposed to be listening to the message.”

“I can do both.”

“That seems like your problem.”

“It becomes yours when I laugh.”

The servant actor said:

“She will.”

“I won't.”

“You already are.”

She was. Barely. Fine.

The servant actor said:

“Put it in your teeth.”

I looked at him. He grinned.

Soot-shirt worker, still by the door, said:

“Don't.”

Fine. I held the letter in my right hand and used the crutch grip with the heel of that hand. Possible. Awkward. Teren watched.

“Can you cross like that?”

“Yes.”

“Do it.”

I entered. Wrong door.

“Other blue,” three people said.

I backed out.

“Both blue.”

The woman said:

“Not to us.”

Second attempt. Correct blue door. Across stage. Three unrailed steps existed at the front. I did not use them. No reason. The chalk table was farther than it looked from the wing. The stage also had more traffic than it appeared to from a chair.

A stool waited just outside my path. A rolled carpet occupied part of the wing. Someone crossed behind the painted wall carrying a lamp. None of this was in the four lines. I reached the chalk table.

Stopped. Read from Teren.

“My lady, a message from Lord…”

I looked at the name. Teren supplied it.

“Varen.”

“Varen.”

The woman held out her hand. I continued reading. She kept holding out her hand. I kept reading.

“Letter,” she said.

“Oh.”

I gave it to her. The servant actor made a small choking sound. Probably laughter. I finished the lines.

“Then go,” Teren said.

“I have another line.”

“After she reads.”

I looked at the page. Yes. Pause. Right. The woman opened the letter. Read silently. Looked at me. I said my final line. Too late.

“Again,” Teren said.

No criticism. Just again. I went back. Third attempt. Correct door. Cross. Line. Letter before she had to ask. Pause. Final line. Exit. I turned toward the wrong side.

“Other way,” Teren said.

I changed direction.

The servant actor said:

“Messenger knows the kingdom. Not the building.”

“Fuck you.”

The woman laughed.

Teren said:

“Again.”

Fourth. I was enjoying this. That was inconvenient. The problem was not the lines. The problem was everything around the lines. Door. Crutches. Letter. Where she stood. When her hand appeared. How long she read.

Where I was supposed to leave. I had four lines and somehow there were twelve failures available. Excellent. Also my right crutch made a sound on one board. Small. Wood tip against a slightly raised seam.

Click. Every crossing. I noticed it on the fifth attempt. Of course I did. I looked down.

Teren said:

“Leave the board.”

“My crutch catches it.”

“Does it stop you?”

“No.”

“Then later.”

“It changes the sound.”

The servant actor said:

“Messenger has hooves.”

I looked at him.

“No horse.”

Nobody understood why that was funny to me. Better. I crossed again. Click. The woman did not react. Neither did anyone else. I tried placing the crutch half an inch left next time. No click.

That made my step worse.

Teren said:

“Why did you do that?”

“Board.”

“Stop.”

Fine. Click returned. Apparently messenger had one hoof. Again. This time I remembered the exit. The woman did not hold out her hand. I almost handed her the letter anyway. Stopped. She looked at me.

I looked at her. She said her line. Then held out her hand. I gave it.

Afterward I said:

“You changed it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I was late.”

“You did that intentionally?”

“No.”

I stared. She shrugged.

“I forgot.”

“That is worse.”

“Did you survive?”

“Yes.”

“Then again.”

Teren said:

“From the argument before entrance.”

I started to leave.

“No. Stay.”

“I am not in the argument.”

“You are outside the door.”

“So I wait?”

“Yes.”

“Doing what?”

“Being outside the door.”

“That is not an action.”

The servant actor said:

“Think messenger thoughts.”

I hated him. I stood behind the blue door. The argument began. Louder than expected. The woman crossed. The man by the door slammed a cup onto the nonexistent table. There was no cup.

He slapped his palm against the chalk rectangle instead.

Teren said:

“Cup.”

Soot-shirt worker tossed him a wooden cup. He caught it. Argument continued. I waited for my line. No. Entrance. I waited for the argument to end. It did not.

The woman shouted:

“Then let him come tell me himself.”

That sounded like entrance. I entered.

Teren said:

“Too early.”

I stopped. The actors did not. The man turned toward me.

“Who the hell are you?”

Not on my page. I looked at Teren. He made a small circular motion. Continue. Right. The woman looked at me too. I had no line yet.

The servant actor, now standing near the wall, whispered:

“Messenger thoughts.”

Fuck him. I looked at the letter. Then at the man.

Then said:

“I was told to deliver this.”

Not the line.

The man snapped:

“Then deliver it.”

I crossed. The woman held out her hand. I gave her the letter. She opened it.

Teren said:

“Now.”

I found the actual first line.

“My lady, a message from Lord Varen.”

The woman looked at the letter already in her hand. Then at me.

“That much I gathered.”

Everyone laughed. I did too. Which made the next line impossible.

Teren said:

“Again from entrance.”

I went back.

“Was that wrong?” I asked.

“Yes,” Teren said.

The woman said:

“It worked.”

Those were different answers. Good.

“Which matters?”

“Right now?” Teren said. “Wrong entrance.”

The woman said:

“Right now? Do it again.”

No philosophy. Fine. We did it again. I waited longer. Correct entrance. Correct line. Correct letter. Correct pause. Correct exit. Boring. Not actually. Cleaner. Then the blue window failed. Same painted window from before.

Or one like it. The evening blue appeared across it. Flickered. Went gray. Nobody stopped. Soot-shirt worker pulled one side lamp lower. Another worker shifted a pale panel. The woman continued arguing with the man.

The window stayed gray. The scene still happened. I watched for half a second too long. Teren tapped my page.

“You're next.”

Right. Messenger. I entered. Correct door. Forgot the letter. I reached the chalk table. Hand empty. The woman held out hers. Nothing. I stopped. Teren said nothing. The servant actor's face became delighted. I could go back.

No. Too late. I looked at the woman. She looked at my empty hand.

Then she said:

“Well?”

I put my hand into my shirt pocket. Nothing there. Obviously.

I said:

“I was told to place it directly in your hands.”

Her eyebrows moved.

“Then?”

“I appear to have been lied to.”

The servant actor folded in half. The woman held it. Barely.

The man said:

“Search him.”

That was not on anything.

“No,” I said.

“Suspicious.”

“I am on crutches.”

“Perfect disguise.”

The woman lost. She laughed.

Teren said:

“Stop.”

Everyone stopped. I expected correction. Teren pointed at the wing.

“Letter.”
