The soot-shirt worker held it up. I had left it on the chair.

“Yes.”

“Get it.”

I went.

The servant actor said:

“Coward.”

“You were not being searched.”

“I would have committed.”

“To what?”

“Anything.”

Probably true. I returned with the letter.

Teren said:

“Again.”

We did it. No one explained what I should have done when the prop vanished. Apparently the answer was not whatever I had done. Also apparently it had not killed the scene. Both could be true.

At the next pause I asked the woman:

“What was I supposed to do?”

“When?”

“Without the letter.”

“Oh.”

She thought.

“Depends.”

“That is not useful.”

“It is exactly useful.”

“What would you have done?”

“If I were you?”

“Yes.”

“Probably swear.”

“Onstage.”

“Quietly.”

I waited. She relented.

“Could have said it was stolen. Could have made him send you back. Could have crossed without handing anything and let me decide. Could have stopped if Teren stopped us.”

“Which is correct?”

“Whichever lets us get to the next thing without making a worse problem.”

“That is not correct.”

“No.”

She smiled.

“It's rehearsal.”

Then somebody called her and she left. That was all the instruction I got. I disliked it. I also wanted another missing letter. The blue window came back while we were halfway through. Nobody applauded.

It was simply blue again. I noticed the effect more this time. Not how. Just that the room looked later. The painted wall had not changed. The window had. The woman's face picked up a little blue on one side.

Then I had to enter. I entered. After six minutes, which was actually closer to thirty, Teren took the pages.

“Done.”

“That was not six minutes.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“We kept using you.”

“That is not a unit of time.”

“It is here.”

The servant actor came over.

“You were terrible.”

“Yes.”

“Better than last time.”

“I did not have a last time.”

“You read merchant.”

“That was seated.”

“Still terrible.”

“Thank you.”

He clapped my shoulder. Not hard.

“Tomorrow?”

There it was again. Everyone in this city had one question.

“I have Hessa.”

“After?”

“I don't know.”

“Fine.”

He left before I could decide whether that was invitation. The woman was arguing with soot-shirt worker about the blue door. Not the window. Door.

“It reads black from the side.”

“It reads blue from front.”

“Half the house is side.”

“Not half.”

“Enough.”

They moved the door. Turned it. Moved a lamp. Still blue. Different blue. I watched. Soot-shirt worker saw me.

“No.”

“I did not say anything.”

“You leaned.”

This was spreading.

“I was looking.”

“Dangerous.”

The woman said:

“Gregory.”

“Yes?”

“Stand there.”

She pointed to a place off the stage. I went.

“Blue?”

I looked. The door was almost black.

“No.”

“Thank you.”

Soot-shirt worker moved the lamp.

“Now?”

“Blue.”

“Done.”

“That seems audience-specific.”

They both looked at me. I regretted speaking.

The woman said:

“It seems blue from where people sit.”

“Yes.”

“That is generally where we need it.”

Right. I shut up. Soot-shirt worker grinned.

“Learning.”

“No.”

“Good.”

They went back to work. I stayed. Not because needed. That distinction was getting weaker. Later somebody gave me a piece of bread. I did not know whose. I ate it. A young crewman carried the chalk table in while I was chewing.

Actual table. I moved my chair without being asked. He put it exactly over the rectangle. Almost. One leg missed by two inches. I noticed. He noticed me noticing.

“Don't.”

“I didn't.”

“Good.”

He shoved the table once. Done. The servant actor dropped the cup again. Different scene. This time nobody laughed because apparently he was supposed to. I could not tell anymore. That was fun. My palms got warm.

I sat before they hurt. Nobody commented. The blue window worked. Then failed once. Then worked. Nobody asked me to care. I did not. Mostly. When I finally left, the soot-shirt worker was changing the hinge on the darker blue door.

I said:

“Wrong blue?”

She said:

“Fuck off, Gregory.”

I laughed all the way to the street. No magic. Tomorrow Hessa. But not yet. For now I had been a messenger for thirty minutes. Badly. I wanted to do it again.
CHAPTER 129
THE STUDENT

The threads were gone. I noticed before I sat down. The frame was gone too. No tile. No copper beside it. No white sleeve. No gray sleeve. Hessa had a cup of tea. This was worse.

“You stopped.”

“Sit.”

“You stopped the thread test.”

“Sit.”

I sat. She checked my hands first. Palms normal. No tenderness from yesterday. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the usual impossible way, mostly heel this morning. Thumb fine. Fingers fine.

Wrist fine. Grip. Again. Fine. Hessa wrote. I waited. She drank tea.

“You stopped.”

“Yes.”

There. I did not like how quickly she said it.

“Why?”

“Because I reviewed the three attempts.”

“And?”

“The apparatus is not giving me enough interpretable signal to justify spending more of your safe attempts on it right now.”

I stared at the empty table.

“One failed replication.”

“One failed replication after two ambiguous attempts.”

“The second was better than ambiguous.”

“It was more interesting.”

“That is not the same word.”

“Correct.”

“The near thread moved toward me during REACH while the far thread didn't.”

“Yes.”

“That is a differential observation.”

“Yes.”

“Then the next test should repeat it.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because we did.”

“Once.”

“Yes.”

“That is not enough.”

“No.”

“Then repeat again.”

“No.”

I hated this. Hessa put down her cup.

“What answer are you trying to get?”

“Whether I moved it.”

“Can this apparatus tell us?”

“Eventually.”

“Maybe.”

“Then why stop?”

“Because your attempts are not free.”

“I am fine.”

“You are fine after the attempts we have done.”

“Yes.”

“That does not make the next ten free.”

“I said one.”

“You will say one after that.”

“Only if it is useful.”

“You currently think another thread attempt is useful.”

“It is.”

“I don't.”

There it was. Jurisdiction. Annoying. Clean. I looked at the empty table again.

“So what did the three tests establish?”

“That thread moves.”

“Excellent.”

“Hessa.”

“You asked.”

She ignored me.

“First, they established that suspended thread in this room is sensitive to more things than we can cheaply isolate.”

“Yes.”

“Air movement. Heat. vibration. twist. static. position. breathing. room traffic.”

“Yes.”

“Second, they established that two threads exposed to much of the same room can still behave differently without your magic.”

“Yes.”

“Third, we observed one movement during REACH that was interesting enough to repeat.”

“Yes.”

“We repeated it.”

“It didn't happen.”

“Correct.”

“That does not disprove it.”

“Correct.”

I stopped. She waited. That was the problem. She was not saying impossible. She was saying not enough. Harder to argue with.

“Fourth,” she said, “the reliable part of all three external attempts was not external.”

I looked at her.

“Your control.”

“Yes.”

“You established the small alteration where instructed. You maintained the underlying draw. You attempted a directional change without broadening into the older response. You did not recruit your hand. You did not chase sensation when the apparatus did something interesting. You RETURNed when told.”

“Mostly.”

“What does mostly mean?”

“I argued afterward.”

“Afterward is allowed.”

Good.

“Your internal sequence is becoming more repeatable than the external observation.”

“Yes.”

“So that is what we test today.”

I looked at the empty space where the frame had been.

“Did you throw it away?”

“No.”

“Where is it?”

“Cabinet.”

“Why?”

“Because if I leave it out, you will spend the entire assessment looking at it.”

“I am looking at where it was.”

“Yes.”

“That proves nothing.”

“It proves I know you.”

I did not answer. She pulled the three old pages from beneath a newer sheet. I recognized the white and gray labels in the margins.

“You kept the notes.”

“Obviously.”

“Show me.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you will argue with my abbreviations.”

“I can read.”

“That has not protected me before.”

“Hessa.”

She turned the first page toward herself, not me.

“Attempt one. Single thread. Baseline movement. One movement toward arm during bounded external question, another later movement with multiple room confounds. No attribution.”

“Two movements.”

“I said one during the bounded question.”

“The other was still during maintained draw.”

“Which is why it is written down.”

Second page.

“Attempt two. Paired threads. Baseline differential behavior demonstrated before draw. During REACH, closer thread moved toward arm while farther did not at that same moment. Later farther moved independently.”

“Yes.”

“Attempt three. Same general setup. During shape, closer moved away, farther moved shortly after. During REACH, no recorded movement from either.”

“Yes.”

She stacked the pages.

“If I only owned the second page, I would repeat.”

“You did.”

“If I owned the first two, I would repeat.”

“You did.”

“If I own all three, I have to ask whether a fourth attempt is the best use of your current tolerance.”

“And you decided no.”

“Yes.”

“What would make you return to it?”

“Better reason.”

“That is vague.”

“A stronger external signal from some other bounded question. Better control. More mature shaping. A reason to think the thread's sensitivity is useful instead of merely noisy.”

“Or time.”

“Possibly.”

“So not abandoned.”

“No.”

That helped more than it should have. I did not want the thread. I wanted the possibility to remain alive. It did. Annoyingly. I looked around.

“No apparatus.”

“Your arm is the apparatus.”

“That sounds medically threatening.”

“It should.”

She brought out the copper. Relief was embarrassing. Not because copper did anything important. Because it belonged to the sequence I knew. Hessa noticed.

“You expected it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“You always use copper.”

“Not always.”

“Recently.”

“Yes.”

“What does that tell you?”

“That you are predictable.”

“Good.”

“No, that was an insult.”

“I know.”

She set it down well away from the old thread position. I watched her choose the place.

“Is that placement part of the test?”

“No.”

“Then why there?”

“Because my tea is here.”

I looked at the tea. Reasonable constraints continued ruining elegant interpretation.

“What question?”

“Whether you can produce the same bounded directional change and RETURN at a different right-forearm target without an external object to pull your attention.”

“That is less interesting.”

“To you.”

“Yes.”

“I know.”

“Why remove the target?”

“Because I want to know whether REACH is currently an instruction you can execute internally, or whether the thread is part of what makes the response happen.”

I sat straighter. That was better. Not thread. Still a question.

“What direction?”

“Not toward the old thread position.”

“Why?”

“Because you have practiced that direction three times.”

“Two.”

“Three external attempts.”

“The first geometry differed.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

She marked my forearm. Charcoal. Small target closer to the upper outer side than the recent wrist-near work. Not elbowward. Not the familiar broad direction. Different. I looked.

“Outward?”

“Toward that mark.”

“There is no object.”

“The mark is an object.”

“External object.”

“No suspended target.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Yes.”

“Can I look at it?”

“Before draw. Not during.”

“Why?”

“Because I want your report, not you steering with your eyes.”

“That is not how mana works.”

“Good. Then it should not matter.”

I disliked that answer. She checked position. Right forearm supported. Hand relaxed. Fingers visible. Copper was present after all. On the other side of the table. Not part of a thread apparatus. Just copper.

Familiar. Hessa placed two fingers above the new charcoal mark.

“Question is small.”

“Yes.”

“One draw.”

“Yes.”

“One shape.”

“Yes.”

“One directional instruction.”

“Yes.”

“One RETURN.”

“Yes.”

“If the response broadens, changes direction, recruits hand or wrist, produces thumb or finger symptoms, produces unusual left response, pain, cold, numbness, weakness, or anything you cannot describe, you stop.”

“Yes.”

“No external effect question.”

“Yes.”

“No casting.”

“Yes.”

“No spell.”

“Yes.”

“No Barrier.”

“Yes.”

“No proving anything.”

I looked at her.

“That one was unnecessary.”

“No.”

“Fine.”

“Draw.”

I did. Minimal. Copper answered. Right forearm. Stable. No hand. No thumb. No left.

“Report.”

I did.

“Shape.”

Localized. The altered region came slower than last time. Not much slower. Enough to notice. I said so.

“Continue only if stable.”

I waited. It settled. Small. Near the charcoal mark but not on it.

“Location?”

I described it. Hessa touched the skin outside the region. No change.

“Hold.”

Held. Then she moved her fingers. Not toward the mark. Away. Two inches farther up and outward. I looked at her.

“That is not the mark.”

“No.”

“You said toward the mark.”

“I changed the instruction.”

“That seems bad.”

“Can you follow it?”

Maybe. That was different. Not REACH toward something. REACH from the altered region toward a direction Hessa indicated in space over my arm. No thread. No fixed destination. Just direction.

“Smallest extension,” she said. “Toward my fingers. No force. Maintain draw.”

I did. Or tried. The near edge sharpened. Wrong edge. Toward the charcoal mark. I stopped.

“Hessa.”

“Report.”

“It went toward the mark.”

“Did you intend that?”

“No.”

“Stop directional instruction. Hold.”

Held. Interesting. Bad. Interesting. She moved her fingers away.

“RETURN.”

I returned. The alteration reduced. Underlying draw remained. No hand. No thumb. No broadening.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Release.”

Released. Hessa checked everything. Again. Fine. I looked at the charcoal mark.

“You tricked me.”

“No.”

“You established a target and then changed it.”

“Yes.”

“That was intentional.”

“Yes.”

“So you were testing whether I was following the instruction or the prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“That is a trick.”

“It is a test.”

“You could have told me.”

“That would change the test.”

I hated that she was right. Mostly.

“What did I do?”

“You shaped near the prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“When I redirected the directional instruction, your first altered edge sharpened toward the prepared target instead of toward my indicated direction.”

“Yes.”

“So I failed.”

“You did not execute the changed direction as instructed.”

“That is failure.”

“For that question, yes.”

Clean. Again. I appreciated it. Also hated it.

“Did the altered region move at all?”

“The edge changed.”

“Toward the prepared mark.”

“By your report.”

“You did not feel it?”

“No.”

“Copper?”

“Changed with draw and shape. Nothing I would distinguish during the directional instruction.”

“So no independent confirmation.”

“No.”

“Could I have simply reported what I expected?”

“Yes.”

I looked at her.

“That is a problem.”

“Yes.”

“You believe me?”

“I believe you are trying to report accurately.”

“That is not the same.”

“No.”

Good. More problems. I had missed having enough problems.

“Can you touch the edge while I do it?”

“Not today.”

“Why?”

“Contact changes sensation.”

“Could still be useful.”

“Yes.”

“Then next time.”

“Maybe.”

“You hate commitments.”

“I make them when I have enough information.”

“That is a lie. You committed to no magic tomorrow very quickly.”

“That decision has excellent evidence.”

I laughed despite myself. She wrote something.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You wrote because I laughed.”

“I wrote because your hand stayed relaxed while you laughed.”

I looked at my right hand. Still open on the support.

“That matters?”

“Maybe.”

“You just did it.”

“What?”

“Made everything information.”

“Everything is information.”

“That is convenient.”

“Only if I don't care what it says.”

I recognized that. She knew I recognized it. Neither of us mentioned the last time.

“What does that mean?”

“I don't know yet.”

“Hessa.”

“It may mean the prepared target strongly organizes what you are doing.”

“Yes.”

“It may mean changing directional instruction after shaping is harder than beginning with the intended direction.”

“Yes.”

“It may mean you anticipated the old sequence.”

“Yes.”

“It may mean my instruction was poor.”

I looked at her.

“Again?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“One attempt.”

“I am fine.”

“One attempt.”

“But this is internal.”

“Yes.”

“And it failed.”

“Yes.”

“So repeat.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because failure is data before it is an invitation.”

That sentence was offensive. I leaned back.

“Tomorrow?”

“No magic.”

“Again?”

“Yes.”

“How many days?”

“One.”

“Then assessment?”

“Yes.”

“What are you going to test?”

“I don't know.”

“You absolutely know.”

“I have questions.”

“Which?”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

She picked up her tea. Cold now, probably.

“Today I learned something I did not know.”

“That I follow charcoal instead of fingers.”

“Possibly.”

“That sounds stupid.”

“It sounds like learning.”

“I knew the charcoal was the target.”

“Exactly.”

I stopped. She drank. I thought about it. I had built the shape around the mark before she changed the instruction. Of course the response favored it. Maybe. Or I had simply failed to redirect.

Or REACH was not direction at all and I had been interpreting noise. Or the thread had mattered. Or Hessa's fingers were a terrible target. Many possibilities. I started listing them. Hessa held up a hand.

“No.”

“I have four.”

“Keep them.”

“I can tell you.”

“I know.”

“You do not know mine.”

“I know enough.”

“That is arrogant.”

“Yes.”

Fair. I looked at my forearm. Charcoal still there. Nothing else.

“Are we farther from external effect than we were?”

“That is not how I would describe it.”

“How would you?”

“We stopped spending attempts on a poor measurement.”

“That is farther.”

“It is different.”

“It feels farther.”

She considered that.

“Yes.”

Good. At least she allowed that. I expected the feeling to disappear once named. It did not. Three days ago I had been staring at a thread that might have moved because of me.

Today Hessa had put the thread in a cabinet and made me fail to follow two fingers. Objectively, that felt like retreat. Also objectively, my arm had done something small on command and then stopped when told.

Again. The second fact was less exciting. It was also the one Hessa trusted. I knew which one I preferred. That did not change which one she trusted. I rubbed neither arm. Kept hands still.

Not because instructed. Habit.

“Am I getting better?”

“At the parts we can currently observe reliably.”

“That is a Hessa answer.”

“Yes.”

“Which parts?”

“Minimal draw. Localized shaping. maintaining draw while altering. RETURN. avoiding the older broad response. avoiding motor recruitment.”

“Directional control?”

“Unclear.”

“External?”

“Unestablished.”

“Casting?”

“No.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

“Barrier?”

“No.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

I sighed. She smiled. Actually smiled. Small. Cruel woman.

“Go live tomorrow.”

“I lived yesterday.”

“You were a messenger.”

I froze. Hessa looked at me.

“How do you know that?”

“Teren's sister buys herbs from the woman downstairs.”

I stared.

“What?”

“She mentioned the theatre had acquired a tall messenger on crutches who forgot his letter.”

I closed my eyes. No. Absolutely not.

“That was rehearsal.”

“I assumed.”

“I was not acquired.”

“I assumed.”

“I am not a messenger.”

“You were yesterday.”

“For thirty minutes.”

“That seems sufficient.”

“This city is too small.”

“Carrow is not small.”

“Then people need to stop talking.”

“No.”

I stood. She pointed at my forearm.

“Wash the charcoal off later.”

“Yes.”

“No magic tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

“No practicing directional attention.”

I stopped.

“What does that mean?”

“You know exactly what it means.”

“I cannot stop looking at things.”

“You can stop sitting at a table trying to recreate today's task without mana.”

“That would not be magic.”

“It would be rehearsal.”

I stared. She raised an eyebrow. I refused to give her that.

“No.”

“Good.”

I left. Outside, the morning had become bright. Not warm. Bright. I walked three streets before realizing I was heading toward the theatre. I stopped. Hessa tomorrow was no magic. Theatre was allowed. That was not why I had turned.

Probably. I looked west. Then east. Then at the street ahead. No test. No conclusion. No thread. My right forearm felt completely ordinary. I went to buy lunch.

At the bread stall, the seller said:

“Messenger.”

I nearly left Carrow.
CHAPTER 130
THE EXTRA

The bread seller called me Messenger again. I ignored him. Mostly. Then I went to the theatre. That proved nothing. The door was open. Inside, nobody needed a messenger. This was disappointing. I had not admitted I wanted to do it again.

Apparently my body had. I stood just inside. Teren was arguing with a page. Not a person. The page. He had three versions open across his knees.

The recurring woman was onstage with the servant actor and another woman I had seen twice but never spoken to. The soot-shirt worker was halfway up a short ladder adjusting something above a painted doorway.

Nobody looked at me. Fine. I went to my usual chair. Basket of fake fruit. Again. I moved it. Teren looked up.

“Gregory.”

“Teren.”

“Chair is wrong.”

“It is the same chair.”

“Not for today.”

“Why?”

“Sightline.”

He pointed two chairs left. I moved. No argument. That felt suspicious. The servant actor noticed.

“Messenger.”

“No.”

“You came back.”

“Yes.”

“For messenger.”

“No.”

“Liar.”

The recurring woman said:

“He forgot the letter. Of course he came back.”

“I did not forget it today.”

“You don't have one.”

“Exactly.”

She smiled. Then went back to the scene. I watched. No messenger. Apparently the play contained other events. Unreasonable. The scene involved three people at a supper table. Actual table today. Not chalk. Wood.

Three cups. One bowl. A plate with nothing on it. The servant actor was supposed to enter late. He kept entering too early. I enjoyed this.

Teren said:

“Again.”

Servant actor returned to the wing.

The woman at the table said:

“You're enjoying this too much.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

They reset. The scene ran. The servant actor entered. Late this time. Better. Then he sat in the wrong chair. The other woman stopped.

“That is mine.”

“Not in the scene.”

“It is now.”

“You have two.”

“I have one body.”

The recurring woman said:

“Keep going.”

They did. The servant actor shifted the cup instead of the chair. The other woman took the cup back. He took the bowl. She took the bowl too.

The scene became a silent war over table objects while the recurring woman delivered a serious line about inheritance. Teren stopped them.

“None of that.”

The servant actor said:

“She started it.”

The other woman said:

“He sat wrong.”

The recurring woman said:

“You're both children.”

Teren said:

“Again.”

Before they reset, a woman from backstage appeared holding the missing belt from earlier.

“Whose?”

Three people answered. Different names. She stared at them.

“Excellent.”

She hung it over the blue door.

The soot-shirt worker shouted:

“Not there.”

“Then come get it.”

“No.”

The belt stayed. The servant actor looked at me.

“Professional environment.”

“Yes.”

“Highly disciplined.”

“Obviously.”

“Do you feel inspired?”

“Deeply.”

He went back to his mark. The belt remained on the door for the next three runs. Nobody who had claimed it took it.

At the fourth run, the woman at the supper table reached the doorway, saw the belt, and used it. She put it around her waist mid-scene. Nobody stopped. The servant actor's eyes widened. She ignored him.

After the scene, somebody backstage shouted:

“That's mine.”

The table woman removed it.

“Then why was it on my door?”

No answer. She handed it to soot-shirt worker. Soot-shirt worker threw it backstage without looking. Someone caught it. I had no idea who owned it. This was apparently less important than everyone had claimed.

I laughed. Nobody cared. Good. The soot-shirt worker climbed down. She had a strip of painted cloth in one hand.

Someone behind her said:

“That's mine.”

She kept walking. The voice followed.

“That's the west-wall strip.”

“It is brown.”

“It is west-wall brown.”

She stopped. Turned. A narrow man with paint on both wrists came out from behind the doorway. He pointed at the strip like she had stolen a child.

“That matches the alley set.”

“It matches this.”

“It absolutely does not.”

They held the strip against the doorway. I looked. Same. Probably. The paint-wrist man looked at me.

“You.”

“No.”

“Which?”

I looked again.

Soot-shirt worker said:

“Don't recruit civilians.”

“He is not civilian anymore.”

“I am absolutely civilian.”

The servant actor called from stage:

“Messenger.”

“Fuck you.”

Paint-wrist man held the strip higher.

“Door or alley?”

I compared. There was a tiny warmer red under the doorway brown. The strip had more gray.

“Alley.”

He pointed at soot-shirt worker.

“Thank you.”

She looked at me.

“Traitor.”

“You asked indirectly.”

“I did not ask.”

“Good.”

She took a different strip from his arm. He objected. She ignored him. This appeared to be a supply system. I liked it. Mostly because nobody was winning. The soot-shirt worker finally turned to me.

“Gregory.”

“Yes.”

“Hold.”

I held. Seated. Learning. She compared the cloth to the painted doorway. Different brown. Slightly. Maybe.

“Wrong?”

I asked.

“Yes.”

“They look the same.”

“No.”

I looked again. One warmer. One grayer.

“Close.”

“Close is wrong under front light.”

“Why?”

She stared at me. I stopped. Not a lesson day. She took the cloth.

“Need darker.”

Went away. I watched rehearsal. No messenger. After maybe twenty minutes, Teren handed me a page. I looked at him.

“What?”

“Read the landlord.”

“Why?”

“Because I need to hear the cut.”

“Where?”

“From chair.”

I looked. Six lines. Older man. Angry about rent. Good. I could do angry about money. Probably. The recurring woman stood at the table. She read opposite me. I started. Too quiet.

“Louder,” Teren said.

Of course. I started again. Louder. Too much. The servant actor covered one ear.

“Landlord is furious.”

“Fuck you.”

Teren said:

“Less.”

I tried. The line sounded normal. The recurring woman answered. I missed the next line because I was looking at the page and not listening. Teren tapped his own copy. I found it. Again.

Second pass better. Third pass, Teren cut half my second line while I was saying it.

“Stop after ‘three months.’”

I stopped. The recurring woman continued. My next line now came sooner. I missed it.

“Again.”

We did. This was not messenger. Still fun. Then Teren changed the cut back.

“Why?”

“Testing.”

“That is rude.”

“Yes.”

The servant actor leaned toward me.

“You hate that word.”

“Testing?”

“Yes.”

“Correct.” We ran the little landlord exchange again. I got through it. Teren took the page.

“Good.”

That meant done. I wanted another. Apparently I had standards now. I sat. The recurring woman went back to the table scene. Someone backstage dropped something metal. Loud. Everyone onstage flinched. The recurring woman did not stop.

She continued the line. The other woman did too. The servant actor turned the flinch into looking toward the doorway. For half a second it looked intentional.

Then Teren said:

“Again from before the drop.”

The metal thing clattered again because somebody kicked it while retrieving it.

The servant actor called:

“Commitment.”

Someone backstage shouted:

“Fuck off.”

Good theatre. The scene restarted. I found myself listening for the drop. It did not happen. Disappointing. At break, the servant actor came over with two cups. One had water. One smelled like something worse.

He gave me water.

“Landlord.”

“No.”

“Messenger Landlord.”

“No.”

“Gregory of Rent.”

“No.”

He sat on the floor. I looked at him.

“Why floor?”

“Chair is cursed.”

“It is a chair.”

“Exactly.”

I drank.

He said:

“You keep coming.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

I looked at him. He waited. Not serious enough to be dangerous.

“It's funny.”

He nodded.

“Mostly.”

“That is not what I said.”

“I know.”

He drank the bad cup. Made a face.

“What is that?”

“Tea.”

“No.”

“Exactly.”

We sat. Around us, people moved furniture. The soot-shirt worker returned with darker cloth. The blue window was not blue. Nobody cared yet. Someone argued about a missing belt. Someone else said the belt was under the red bench.

There were two red benches. Apparently this building had learned nothing from blue doors. I smiled. The servant actor saw.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Dangerous.”

He stood. Break over. I expected to keep sitting. Instead the recurring woman pointed at me.

“Gregory.”

“Yes?”

“Stand there.”

She pointed near the painted doorway. I stood.

“What am I?”

“Person.”

“That is broad.”

“You can manage.”

The servant actor said:

“Debatable.”

She ignored him.

“When she crosses, move aside.”

The other woman stood at the table.

“Why?”

“Because she needs the path.”

“That is not acting.”

“No.”

Good. I stood. The scene began. The other woman crossed. I moved aside. Too early. Also wrong direction. I had moved toward the painted doorway because it was closer. She had planned to cross behind me.

Now I was in the path twice. She stopped.

“Why are you following me?”

“I am avoiding you.”

“You are extremely bad at it.”

“I noticed.”

“Again.”

Teren did not even say it. She did. Apparently everyone had authority over again now. We reset. The second attempt I waited too long. She had to angle around my right crutch. Not dangerous.

Ugly. She finished the cross anyway.

Then turned at the table and said:

“Your crutch is louder than you are.”

“That seems false.”

“Not from here.”

Teren looked up.

“She's right.”

“About volume?”

“Yes.”

“This is becoming personal.”

The servant actor said:

“Landlord Messenger Furniture has a sound problem.”

“I will kill you.”

“Not in this scene.”

“Again.”

I went back. She changed path. I moved again. Now I was in her way. She stopped. Looked at me.

“Choose.”

“I was getting out of the way.”

“Once.”

Right. Again. This time I waited until she committed to a path. Moved once. Fine. Then the servant actor entered from behind me and nearly hit my crutch. He avoided it. Kept scene.

Afterward he said:

“Your leg is in my kingdom.”

“Crutch.”

“Same problem.”

“Then use another door.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Mine.”

Of course.

Teren said:

“Gregory, half a step left.”

I moved. Servant actor tried entrance. Clear.

“Again.”

We repeated. That was all. I had become scenery with opinions. Excellent.

Then the recurring woman added:

“When I say ‘bring him in,’ cross to table.”

“Who?”

“You.”

“As what?”

“Person.”

“That is not enough.”

“It is today.”

“What do I do at table?”

“Stand.”

“Why?”

“Because I am talking to you.”

“Do I have lines?”

“No.”

The servant actor said:

“Messenger has been demoted.”

I looked at him.

“Landlord outranks messenger.”

“Person is below both.”

Unclear hierarchy. We ran it.

The woman said:

“Bring him in.”

I crossed. Too fast.

“Again.”

Too slow.

“Again.”

I stopped at wrong side of table.

“Again.”

I looked at Teren. He was not smiling. Not annoyed either. Just pages. Again. I crossed. Stopped where she could see me without turning away from the other actor. She said her line to me.

I had no response. I looked at her. She continued. That was apparently correct. Strange. Next run she stood closer. I stopped in the old place. Now I was too far away. She looked at the distance between us.

Then at me. I stayed. She said the line louder.

Afterward:

“Why didn't you move closer?”

“You moved.”

“Yes.”

“You said stop there.”

“I said stop where I can talk to you.”

“That is not a location.”

“It is today.”

I looked at Teren. He was writing. No help.

“So I choose?”

“Yes.”

“Based on what?”

“Where I am.”

“That changes.”

“Yes.”

“That is terrible.”

She smiled.

“Again.”

I moved closer next time. Too close. She stepped back while continuing the scene. I noticed and adjusted half a step. Teren did not stop us. That was apparently acceptable. Not correct. Acceptable. The distinction was becoming irritatingly useful.

Next pass I nodded. She stopped.

“No.”

“What?”

“Don't.”

“Why?”

“Because then I have to answer the nod.”

“That makes no sense.”

“It makes enough.”

I stared. She smiled.

“Again.”

Fine. No nod. Just stand. Harder than expected. My face wanted to do something. My body wanted to acknowledge. Instead I stood. She spoke. I listened. Then she turned away. Scene moved. Teren did not stop.

That felt like success. Tiny. Embarrassing. Good. Later, the soot-shirt worker needed the path. I moved before she asked. She noticed.

“Learning.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

She carried the darker cloth up the ladder. The painted doorway changed almost imperceptibly. Under the front lamp, the patch disappeared. I could not see where old brown ended and new began. That was satisfying.

Not magic. Paint. Good. The afternoon kept going. No messenger. I stopped caring. Mostly. I read landlord twice more when Teren needed it. I stood as Person during three runs. One time I forgot to move when the other woman crossed.

She shoulder-checked me lightly. Kept going. I apologized after.

She said:

“Move next time.”

“Yes.”

That was all. One time the servant actor came through his door too fast and caught the edge of the painted flat with his sleeve. The flat shifted. Soot-shirt worker grabbed it. The actor kept going.

I almost looked at the flat. Did not. Because the recurring woman was speaking to me. I stayed where I was. Afterward I looked. The flat was fine. Soot-shirt worker had already wedged it.

No one praised me for not turning around. Obviously. It was not impressive. That felt good too. The next run the flat did not shift. The run after that, the cup rolled off the table.

Different failure. The recurring woman caught it against her skirt with one hand and kept speaking. The other woman took it from her without looking. Servant actor reached for it one line later because his hand expected the cup to be there.

Nothing. He converted the reach into pointing. Nobody laughed. The scene continued.

Afterward he said:

“I saved that.”

The recurring woman said:

“You nearly murdered a cup.”

“I saved the scene.”

“You pointed.”

“Heroically.”

Teren said:

“Again.”

I laughed. Servant actor pointed at me.

“See? Audience.”

“I am not audience.”

“You laughed.”

“Against my will.”

“Counts.”

I did not know whether it counted. I did know I wanted the next run. At the end Teren collected pages.

“Tomorrow?”

“Hessa.”

He nodded. No after. Interesting. The recurring woman passed me carrying the empty plate. She stopped. Looked at me.

“You came back.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

That was all. Small. Ordinary. Somehow better than being needed. I liked that.

Then:

“Messenger.”

“I was not messenger.”

“Landlord?”

“Briefly.”

“Person?”

“Yes.”

She nodded solemnly.

“Promotion.”

“Fuck you.”

She laughed. I left. My palms were warm. Right calf tired. Not bad. Residual limb quiet. I sat on the low wall outside before walking home. Not because ordered. Because I wanted to. People passed.

Nobody called me Messenger. Excellent. Then the bread seller across the street saw me. He raised one hand. I raised a finger. He laughed. I did too. No magic today. Tomorrow Hessa. Today I had been a landlord, a person, and occasionally furniture.

None of them mattered. I wanted to go back.
